title: About the course and about me
text:
What an actuary does
Insurers sell a promise: if something bad happens, we pay. Someone has to decide the price of that promise. An actuary prices it with probability. How often does a car crash? How large is a typical claim? How much money must be set aside so the company survives a terrible year?
That is the content of this course with the insurance removed: probability first, then statistics for estimating it from data.

section: What I researched: care for the elderly
text:
What I researched: care for the elderly
My data came from nursing homes in the canton of Geneva: more than 21,000 residents, followed from 1996 to 2018. An insurer or a nursing home has to answer three questions. How long will a resident stay? How much care will they need while they are there? What will it cost? All three are probability questions with real money behind them.
I wrote three papers on them with Joël Wagner (University of Lausanne).

Duration and intensity of care (Annals of Actuarial Science, 2023, with M. Bladt and M. Fuino). An accelerated failure time model for how long people stay, and beta regression for how intensive the care is.
Health profiles (Insurance: Mathematics and Economics, 2024). Spectral clustering finds eight typical profiles of residents, and multinomial logistic regression shows what decides the profile.
Costs over time (Insurance: Mathematics and Economics, 2025). A multi-state Markov model: a resident moves between four care levels, from nearly independent to severely dependent, and each level has a price.

You will meet the same ideas here in simpler clothes. The Markov model is conditional probability, repeated: given that a resident is in state 2 today, what is the chance of state 3 tomorrow? That is Lecture 2. Length of stay is a random variable with a distribution, an expectation and a variance. That is Lectures 3 to 5. Regression and estimation from data come in module 3.

section: Why this matters for a business student
text:
Why this matters for a business student
Pricing, credit risk, inventory, quality control, A/B tests, surveys. All of them ask the same thing: how sure can we be, given what we know?
Take a bank that has just approved 1,000 loans. Some borrowers will not pay back, and nobody knows which ones.
In module 2 we work before any data. If each loan defaults with probability \(p\), how many defaults should the bank plan for, and how far from that number can the real count be? In module 3 the bank has six months of real data. How well does it know \(p\), and when is a change in the default rate more than bad luck?

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.1 Experiments and outcomes
Ilya opens a coffee stand near Paveletskaya station and bakes 30 croissants every morning. Will he sell all of them? Nobody knows. Some days he sells 22, some days all 30 by ten o’clock. A better question is how likely it is that he sells at least 25, because that one he can plan around: how much dough to prepare, whether to hire a second person for the rush.
Probability theory is the language for questions of this second kind. Before we can compute anything we need a vocabulary: what exactly is “an outcome”, what is “an event”, and what rules a probability must obey. Then we will see how far plain counting takes us.
The list of outcomes is something you choose. It depends on what you decide to record.
Experiment 3 deserves a second look. If Ilya sold croissants without limit, the space would be \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), infinite but still a list. Experiment 4 is a different kind of infinity: you cannot number the possible waiting times one by one. We will keep this difference in mind until Lecture 4.
A habit to avoid: choosing \(\Omega\) too coarse. If you record only “customer 1 buys” and “customer 2 buys” as one number (how many bought, 0, 1 or 2), you lose the difference between \(BL\) and \(LB\), and the three remaining outcomes are no longer equally likely. We will meet exactly this trap with dice in Section 1.4.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
Definition 1.1 (Random experiment and sample space) A random experiment is a procedure whose result we cannot predict with certainty, but whose possible results we can list in advance. Each possible result is an outcome. The set of all outcomes is the sample space, written \(\Omega\).



Example 1.1 (Four experiments, four sample spaces)  

One customer walks up to Ilya’s stand and either buys something or leaves. \(\Omega=\{\text{buys},\ \text{leaves}\}\).
Two customers walk up one after another. We now record both, in order: \(\Omega=\{BB,\ BL,\ LB,\ LL\}\), where \(B\) means buys and \(L\) means leaves. Four outcomes, and \(BL\) is not the same as \(LB\).
We count the croissants sold in a day. \(\Omega=\{0,1,2,\dots,30\}\).
We measure how many minutes a customer waits in the queue. \(\Omega=[0,\infty)\). This sample space is not a list at all, it is a whole interval of numbers.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.2 Events and set operations

Definition 1.2 (Event) An event is a set of outcomes, a subset \(A\subseteq\Omega\). We say that \(A\) occurs if the outcome of the experiment belongs to \(A\).

The whole space \(\Omega\) is the sure event, since something always happens. The empty set \(\varnothing\) is the impossible event.
Events are sets, so we combine them with set operations. Each operation has a plain-language reading, and you should be able to go both ways without thinking.



Table 1.1: Set operations on events





Notation

Occurs when




\(A\cup B\)

at least one of them occurs

Figure 1.1 shows them as regions of a rectangle. The rectangle is \(\Omega\).








Figure 1.1: The four operations from Table 1.1. The shaded region is the event named above each panel.






Example 1.2 (Promo code and mobile app) An online store picks one customer at random from yesterday’s orders. Let \(A\) be “the customer used a promo code” and \(B\) “the customer ordered through the mobile app”. Then \(A\cap B^c\) is an order with a promo code placed on the website, and \((A\cup B)^c\) is an order with no promo code that was not placed in the app. The event \(A^c\cap B^c\) reads the same way, and that is no coincidence: the two events are equal, and the next result says why.


Definition 1.3 (Mutually exclusive events, partition) Events \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) if \(A\cap B=\varnothing\): they cannot occur together. Events \(H_1,\dots,H_n\) form a partition of \(\Omega\) if they are pairwise mutually exclusive and \(H_1\cup\dots\cup H_n=\Omega\). Exactly one of them occurs.

For any event \(A\), the pair \(A\) and \(A^c\) is the simplest partition. Partitions come back in Lecture 2, in the law of total probability.

Theorem 1.1 (De Morgan’s laws) \[
(A\cup B)^c = A^c\cap B^c,\qquad (A\cap B)^c = A^c\cup B^c .
\]

Proof
An outcome is outside \(A\cup B\) exactly when it is outside \(A\) and outside \(B\), which is the first law. The second law is the same sentence with “and” and “or” swapped. In words: “not (promo or app)” is “no promo and no app”. This is the equality in Example 1.2.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.3 The axioms of probability
What should a probability be? Think of the share of days on which an event happens, over a very long run. That share is never negative, it equals 1 for the sure event, and for events that cannot happen together the shares add up. Kolmogorov turned these three observations into the definition.

Definition 1.4 (Probability) A probability assigns to every event \(A\) a number \(\Prob(A)\) so that

\(\Prob(A)\ge 0\);
\(\Prob(\Omega)=1\);
if \(A_1, A_2,\dots\) are pairwise mutually exclusive, then \(\Prob(A_1\cup A_2\cup\dots)=\Prob(A_1)+\Prob(A_2)+\dots\)


For an infinite sample space such as \([0,\infty)\) one cannot assign probabilities to literally every subset, and the full theory restricts the events allowed. We will not need that. Everything in this course that looks like an event is an event.
Everything else follows from these three lines.

Theorem 1.2 (Consequences of the axioms) For any events \(A\) and \(B\):

\(\Prob(\varnothing)=0\).
\(\Prob(A^c)=1-\Prob(A)\).
If \(A\subseteq B\), then \(\Prob(A)\le\Prob(B)\). In particular \(\Prob(A)\le 1\).
\(\Prob(A\cup B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cap B)\).



Proof. For (1): take \(A_1=\Omega\) and \(A_2=A_3=\dots=\varnothing\) in axiom 3. They are mutually exclusive and their union is \(\Omega\), so \(\Prob(\Omega)=\Prob(\Omega)+\Prob(\varnothing)+\Prob(\varnothing)+\dots\) The left side is finite, and every term on the right is non-negative, so \(\Prob(\varnothing)=0\).
For (2): \(A\) and \(A^c\) are mutually exclusive and \(A\cup A^c=\Omega\), so by axioms 3 and 2, \(\Prob(A)+\Prob(A^c)=\Prob(\Omega)=1\).
For (3): if \(A\subseteq B\), then \(B\) is the union of the mutually exclusive events \(A\) and \(B\cap A^c\). So \(\Prob(B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B\cap A^c)\ge\Prob(A)\), since the last term is non-negative. Taking \(B=\Omega\) gives \(\Prob(A)\le 1\).
For (4): write \(A\cup B\) as two mutually exclusive pieces, \(A\) and \(B\cap A^c\). Then \(\Prob(A\cup B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B\cap A^c)\). Also \(B\) splits into \(B\cap A\) and \(B\cap A^c\), so \(\Prob(B\cap A^c)=\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cap B)\). Substitute.

Property (4) is the formula you will use most often, and the mistake you will make most often is to forget the last term. Add \(\Prob(A)\) and \(\Prob(B)\), and the outcomes in both events are counted twice. For three events the correction goes one step further:
\[
\Prob(A\cup B\cup C)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)+\Prob(C)-\Prob(A\cap B)-\Prob(A\cap C)-\Prob(B\cap C)+\Prob(A\cap B\cap C).
\tag{1.1}\]

Example 1.3 (Promo code and mobile app, with numbers) In a hypothetical online store 40% of orders use a promo code, 55% come through the mobile app, and 20% do both. Take \(A\) and \(B\) as in Example 1.2. Find the probability that a random order

uses a promo code or the app;
uses neither;
comes through the app without a promo code.

Solution. (a) By Theorem 1.2(4), \(\Prob(A\cup B)=0.40+0.55-0.20=0.75\). (b) This is the complement of (a): \(\Prob\big((A\cup B)^c\big)=1-0.75=0.25\). (c) \(\Prob(B\cap A^c)=\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cap B)=0.55-0.20=0.35\).
A check: promo only (0.20), app only (0.35), both (0.20) and neither (0.25) are four mutually exclusive pieces, and \(0.20+0.35+0.20+0.25=1\).

The complement rule is the tool for any “at least one” question. Computing the probability that something happens at least once is usually hard, while the probability that it never happens is often a single product. Then subtract from 1. We will use it in the lecture on counting and again in every later lecture.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.4 Classical probability
The axioms say what a probability must satisfy, and not how to find it. The oldest recipe is the one for games of chance.

Definition 1.5 (Classical probability) Suppose \(\Omega\) has finitely many outcomes and, by the symmetry of the experiment, all of them are equally likely. Then for every event \(A\) \[
\Prob(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}=\frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{number of outcomes in }\Omega}.
\]

Check that this satisfies the axioms: it is never negative, \(\Prob(\Omega)=1\), and for mutually exclusive events the counts add up. So it is a legitimate probability. The entire difficulty is hidden in the phrase “equally likely”.

Example 1.4 (Two dice) Roll a red die and a blue die. The sample space has 36 outcomes \((i,j)\), where \(i\) is the red number and \(j\) the blue number, and all 36 are equally likely. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
Solution. The outcomes with sum 7 are \((1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)\). There are 6 of them (Figure 1.2), so \(\Prob(\text{sum}=7)=6/36=1/6\).









Figure 1.2: The 36 equally likely outcomes of two dice. The six outcomes with sum 7 are highlighted.





Now the trap. The possible sums are \(2,3,\dots,12\), eleven values. Many students conclude that each sum has probability \(1/11\). It does not. The sum 7 can happen in six ways and the sum 2 in only one, \((1,1)\). The eleven sums are the coarse sample space we warned about in Section 1.1, and its outcomes are not equally likely. The 36 pairs are. When you use Definition 1.5, first ask: what is the finest description of the experiment in which every outcome is equally likely?
The same trap catches grown-ups. Toss a fair coin twice and ask for exactly one head. The answer is \(2/4=1/2\) (outcomes \(HT\) and \(TH\)), not \(1/3\).
Classical probability is the right tool for dice, cards, lotteries and drawing a random name from a list. It is the wrong tool for most business questions. “A customer either buys or does not, so the probability is 1/2” is the same mistake in a suit: the two outcomes are not equally likely, and for such cases the probability has to come from data or from a model. That is what the rest of the course is about.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.5 Counting
To use Definition 1.5 we must count outcomes, and the lists get too long to write out. A lottery with 6 numbers out of 45 has millions of outcomes. Three rules cover almost everything we need.

Theorem 1.3 (Product rule) If a procedure has \(k\) stages, the first stage can be done in \(n_1\) ways, the second in \(n_2\) ways (whatever happened in the first), and so on, then the whole procedure can be done in \(n_1 n_2\cdots n_k\) ways.

Proof
After the first stage there are \(n_1\) possible situations. Each of them continues in \(n_2\) ways, which gives \(n_1n_2\) pairs of choices. Each pair continues in \(n_3\) ways, which gives \(n_1n_2n_3\) triples, and so on up to stage \(k\).


Example 1.5 (PIN codes) A bank card has a four-digit PIN. Each of the four positions has 10 choices, so there are \(10^4=10\,000\) PINs. If the digits must all be different, the first position has 10 choices, the second 9, then 8 and 7, giving \(10\cdot 9\cdot 8\cdot 7=5040\).
A thief who guesses one PIN at random hits it with probability \(1/10\,000\).

The two PIN counts are of different kinds. With repeats allowed, each digit is chosen afresh and we get \(n^k\) (here \(10^4\)); this is an ordered selection with repetition, and the product rule is all it needs. Without repeats the choices shrink by one at each step. That case, and two related ones, come up so often that they have classical names. Write \(n!=n(n-1)\cdots 2\cdot 1\) (“\(n\) factorial”), with \(0!=1\).

Definition 1.6 (Permutation) A permutation of \(n\) distinct objects is an ordering of all of them in a row. There are \(n!\) permutations (Theorem 1.4).
Kemal drives a delivery van and has 5 shops to visit this morning. Each route is a permutation of the 5 shops, so he can choose among \(5!=120\) routes. Exercise 3 at the end of the chapter, the order of six job interviews, is also about permutations.


Definition 1.7 (Arrangement) An arrangement of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects (\(k\le n\)) is an ordered selection without repetition: we pick a first, a second, up to a \(k\)-th, and no object is used twice. There are \[
\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)
\] arrangements (Theorem 1.4).
A supermarket has 12 brands of tea and 3 slots at eye level: left, middle and right. Putting three brands into the three slots is an arrangement, and there are \(12\cdot11\cdot10=1320\) of them. The PINs with four different digits in Example 1.5 are arrangements of 4 digits from 10: \(10!/6!=5040\).

A permutation is the arrangement with \(k=n\), and then the formula gives \(n!/0!=n!\). That is one reason to set \(0!=1\).

Definition 1.8 (Combination) A combination of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects (\(0\le k\le n\)) is an unordered selection without repetition, that is, a subset of size \(k\). The number of combinations is written \(\binom{n}{k}\), read “\(n\) choose \(k\)” and called the binomial coefficient. Its formula is Equation 1.2 below.
The same supermarket picks 3 of its 12 tea brands for a weekend discount. Now the three brands form a set, and nothing is first or last. The lottery in Example 1.6 and the inspector’s sample in Example 1.7 are combinations too.

Other textbooks use other words and symbols for the same things, and you should recognise them. An arrangement is also called a \(k\)-permutation, a partial permutation or a variation, and other books write \(A_n^k\), \(P(n,k)\) or \({}_nP_k\) for the number of them. For \(\binom{n}{k}\) other books write \(C_n^k\) or \({}_nC_k\). Be careful with the word “arrangement” in English books: many of them use it loosely for any ordering, a full permutation included. In this course it always means an ordered selection of \(k\) from \(n\).

Theorem 1.4 (Orderings and selections) From \(n\) distinct objects:

There are \(n!\) permutations.
There are \(\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\) arrangements of \(k\) objects.
There are \[
\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}
\tag{1.2}\] combinations of \(k\) objects.

Parts 2 and 3 are linked by \(\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}=k!\binom{n}{k}\).


Proof. Part 1 is the product rule with \(n,n-1,\dots,1\) choices. Part 2 is the same with \(k\) stages. For part 3, each combination of \(k\) objects appears in the count of part 2 exactly \(k!\) times, once for each permutation of its \(k\) objects. So the number of arrangements is \(k!\binom{n}{k}\). Divide by \(k!\).

In the tea example, \(1320=3!\cdot 220\): each set of three discounted brands can be put into the three eye-level slots in \(3!=6\) ways, and \(\binom{12}{3}=220\).
Two useful facts: \(\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}\) (choosing who goes in is the same as choosing who stays out) and \(\binom{n}{0}=\binom{n}{n}=1\).
The practical question is always the same: does order matter? Swap two chosen items. If the result is a different outcome, count arrangements. If it is the same outcome, count combinations. Three candidates for gold, silver and bronze: ordered, \(10\cdot9\cdot8=720\) from ten. Three candidates for a project team: unordered, \(\binom{10}{3}=120\). Check: \(720/3!=120\).

Example 1.6 (A 6-from-45 lottery) You pick 6 different numbers from 1 to 45, and the draw produces 6 numbers. Order is irrelevant. The number of possible draws is \[
\binom{45}{6}=\frac{45\cdot44\cdot43\cdot42\cdot41\cdot40}{720}=8\,145\,060,
\] so a single ticket wins the jackpot with probability \(1/8\,145\,060\approx 1.2\cdot10^{-7}\). If you bought a ticket every week, you would wait on average about 157 000 years.

The next example is the one to remember. It is a typical quality-control calculation, and we will see it again in Lecture 4 as the hypergeometric distribution.

Example 1.7 (Expired packs) A warehouse shelf holds 20 packs of yoghurt, and 3 of them are past their date. An inspector takes 4 packs at random. Find the probability that

exactly one is expired;
none is expired;
at least one is expired.

Solution. Order does not matter, so \(|\Omega|=\binom{20}{4}=4845\). For (a), choose 1 of the 3 expired packs and 3 of the 17 good ones, which is \(\binom{3}{1}\binom{17}{3}=3\cdot 680=2040\) outcomes (product rule). So \(\Prob=2040/4845\approx 0.421\). For (b), all 4 come from the 17 good packs: \(\binom{17}{4}/\binom{20}{4}=2380/4845\approx 0.491\). For (c), use the complement: \(1-0.491=0.509\).

Notice that the inspector checks four packs out of twenty and finds a problem in barely more than half of the cases, although 15% of the packs are bad. Sampling a small part of a batch is a weak control. That is a point about sample sizes, and we will come back to it in module 3.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
1.6 Geometric probability
Sometimes the outcomes cannot be listed at all: a moment in time, a point on a map. If we pick one “at random”, the natural meaning is that every place is equally good, and probability becomes proportional to size.

Definition 1.9 (Geometric probability) Let \(\Omega\) be a segment, a region in the plane, or a region in space, with finite length, area or volume. An outcome is chosen uniformly at random from \(\Omega\) if for every event \(A\subseteq\Omega\) \[
\Prob(A)=\frac{\text{size of }A}{\text{size of }\Omega},
\] where “size” means length, area or volume.


Example 1.8 (A courier in a two-hour window) A courier promises to arrive between 10:00 and 12:00, and the exact moment is uniform over those 120 minutes. You will be out from 10:30 to 11:15. The probability that the courier comes while you are out is the length of the interval (45 minutes) divided by 120: \(45/120=3/8\).

The more interesting case has two random moments.

Example 1.9 (Two people, one café) Zarina and Oksana agree to meet at a café between 12:00 and 13:00. Each arrives at a random moment of that hour, independently of the other, and waits 15 minutes before leaving. What is the probability that they meet?
Solution. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the arrival times in minutes after 12:00. The pair \((x,y)\) is a uniform point in the square \([0,60]\times[0,60]\), area 3600. They meet when \(|x-y|\le 15\), which is the band around the diagonal in Figure 1.3. It is easier to find the area outside the band: two right triangles with legs \(60-15=45\), each of area \(45^2/2\). The band has area \(3600-45^2=1575\), so \[
\Prob(\text{meet})=\frac{3600-45^2}{3600}=1-\Big(\frac{45}{60}\Big)^2=\frac{7}{16}\approx 0.44.
\]









Figure 1.3: All pairs of arrival times (Example 1.9). They meet when the point lies in the shaded band \(|x-y|\le 15\).





People find 7/16 low. Fifteen minutes feels generous, and yet they miss each other more than half of the time. Writing the meeting problem on the board as a square is the entire trick: two numbers become one point.
A remark that will matter in Lecture 4. In a geometric setting the probability of any single point is zero, because a point has no length. The probability that the courier arrives at exactly 10:47:12.000 is 0, and still she arrives at some moment. Probability zero does not mean impossible once \(\Omega\) is a continuum.

title: 1  Events, probability and counting
text:
Exercises

Two dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
A manager says: “The chance of a delay at the supplier is 0.5, the chance of a customs problem is 0.6, and they never happen together.” What is wrong with that statement?
Six candidates, including Ilya and Priya, are interviewed in random order. What is the probability that Ilya is interviewed before Priya? That the two are interviewed one right after the other, in either order?
A password has 4 characters, each a lowercase letter. How many passwords have at least one repeated letter? (Use the complement.)
A point is chosen uniformly in a square of side 2. What is the probability that it lies within distance 1 of the centre?

Answers: (1) \(1/6\). (2) Two mutually exclusive events with probabilities 0.5 and 0.6 would give \(\Prob(A\cup B)=1.1>1\). (3) \(1/2\); \(\frac{5\cdot 2\cdot 4!}{6!}=1/3\). (4) \(26^4-26\cdot25\cdot24\cdot23=456\,976-358\,800=98\,176\). (5) \(\pi/4\approx 0.785\).
The full practice is in Seminar 1.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
2.1 Conditional probability
Go back to the online store of Example 1.3: 40% of orders use a promo code, 55% come through the mobile app, and 20% do both. Priya, a marketing analyst there, sees that a customer has just opened the app. Should she still count on a 40% chance that this order uses a promo code?
No. Among app orders, the ones with a promo code make up 0.20 out of 0.55, so the chance is \[
\frac{0.20}{0.55}\approx 0.36 .
\] Knowing “this is an app order” moved the probability from 0.40 to about 0.36. A small move, but a real one, and that one division is the starting point for everything below: conditional probability, independence, the law of total probability and Bayes’ theorem.
Read \(\Prob(A\mid B)\) as “the probability of \(A\) given \(B\)”. The idea is in Figure 2.1. Once we know that \(B\) has occurred, every outcome outside \(B\) is ruled out. \(B\) becomes the new sample space, and the only part of \(A\) that can still happen is \(A\cap B\). Dividing by \(\Prob(B)\) rescales things so that the new space has total probability 1 again.
Figure 2.1: Conditioning on \(B\). Left: the whole sample space, with \(A\cap B\) shaded. Right: once we know \(B\) occurred, everything outside \(B\) (grey) is ruled out, and \(\Prob(A\mid B)\) is the share of \(B\) taken by \(A\cap B\).
When all outcomes are equally likely (Definition 1.5), the division turns into a ratio of counts: \(\Prob(A\mid B)=|A\cap B|/|B|\). Roll the two dice of Lecture 1 (Example 1.4), one red and one blue, and suppose you can see only the red one. It shows a 6. Now the sum is at least 10 exactly when the blue die shows 4, 5 or 6, which is 3 of the 6 remaining outcomes, so the probability is \(1/2\). Before you looked at the red die it was \(6/36=1/6\).
Parts (a) and (b) answer different questions. (a) asks: among app orders, what share used a promo code? (b) asks: among promo-code orders, what share came through the app? The numerator is the same, the denominator is not. Swapping \(\Prob(A\mid B)\) and \(\Prob(B\mid A)\) is the most common mistake of this whole lecture, and you will find it in newspapers too. “Half of promo-code users order through the app” is true here. “Half of app users use a promo code” is false: it is 36%.
Part (c) is no accident. For a fixed \(B\), conditional probabilities obey all the rules of Lecture 1.
The complement goes in front of the bar, never behind it. \(\Prob(A\mid B^c)\) is not \(1-\Prob(A\mid B)\). In the store, \(\Prob(A\mid B^c)=\Prob(A\cap B^c)/\Prob(B^c)=0.20/0.45\approx 0.444\), while \(1-\Prob(A\mid B)\approx 0.636\). Two unrelated numbers.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
Definition 2.1 (Conditional probability) Let \(B\) be an event with \(\Prob(B)>0\). The conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is \[
\Prob(A\mid B)=\frac{\Prob(A\cap B)}{\Prob(B)}.
\]





Example 2.1 (Promo code given app, and the other way round) Take the store of Example 1.3, with \(A\) “the order uses a promo code” and \(B\) “the order comes through the app”. Find

\(\Prob(A\mid B)\);
\(\Prob(B\mid A)\);
\(\Prob(A^c\mid B)\).

Solution. (a) \(\Prob(A\mid B)=0.20/0.55=4/11\approx 0.364\). (b) \(\Prob(B\mid A)=0.20/0.40=0.50\). (c) The app orders without a promo code have probability \(\Prob(A^c\cap B)=0.35\), found in Example 1.3(c). So \(\Prob(A^c\mid B)=0.35/0.55\approx 0.636\). Notice that (a) and (c) add up to 1.




Theorem 2.1 (Conditional probability is a probability) Fix an event \(B\) with \(\Prob(B)>0\). Then \(A\mapsto\Prob(A\mid B)\) satisfies the three axioms of Definition 1.4. So every rule of Theorem 1.2 holds for it, for example \(\Prob(A^c\mid B)=1-\Prob(A\mid B)\) and \(\Prob(A_1\cup A_2\mid B)=\Prob(A_1\mid B)+\Prob(A_2\mid B)-\Prob(A_1\cap A_2\mid B)\).

Proof
Axiom 1: \(\Prob(A\cap B)\ge 0\) and \(\Prob(B)>0\), so the ratio is non-negative. Axiom 2: \(\Prob(\Omega\mid B)=\Prob(\Omega\cap B)/\Prob(B)=\Prob(B)/\Prob(B)=1\). Axiom 3: if \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) are pairwise mutually exclusive, so are \(A_1\cap B, A_2\cap B,\dots\), and their union is \((A_1\cup A_2\cup\dots)\cap B\). Apply axiom 3 for \(\Prob\) to these pieces and divide by \(\Prob(B)\).

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
2.2 Multiplication rule
Turn the definition around and you get \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(B)\,\Prob(A\mid B)\). In practice this is how most joint probabilities are found. We think in steps: first \(B\) happens, then \(A\) happens given \(B\).

Theorem 2.2 (Multiplication rule) If \(\Prob(A)>0\) and \(\Prob(B)>0\), then \[
\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\,\Prob(B\mid A)=\Prob(B)\,\Prob(A\mid B).
\] More generally, if \(\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1})>0\), then \[
\Prob(A_1\cap A_2\cap\dots\cap A_n)=\Prob(A_1)\,\Prob(A_2\mid A_1)\,\Prob(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2)\cdots\Prob(A_n\mid A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1}).
\tag{2.1}\]


Proof. The first line is Definition 2.1 multiplied by \(\Prob(A)\), or by \(\Prob(B)\). For Equation 2.1, write each conditional probability on the right as a fraction: \[
\Prob(A_1)\cdot\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2)}{\Prob(A_1)}\cdot\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)}{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2)}\cdots\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n)}{\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1})}.
\] Each numerator cancels the next denominator, and only \(\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n)\) is left. The denominators are positive: each of them is the probability of an event that contains \(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1}\), so it is at least \(\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1})>0\) by Theorem 1.2(3).

Equation 2.1 reads like a story. First \(A_1\) happens. Then \(A_2\) happens, given \(A_1\). Then \(A_3\), given both earlier ones. Each factor answers one question: what is the chance of the next step, given everything so far?

Example 2.2 (Birthdays, one person at a time) Kemal’s department has 10 people. Ignore 29 February, and assume each person’s birthday is equally likely to be any of the 365 days, whatever the others’ birthdays are. What is the probability that all 10 birthdays are different?
Solution. Line the people up. Let \(A_k\) be “person \(k\) has a birthday different from persons \(1,\dots,k-1\)”. Person 1 has nobody to clash with. Given that persons \(1,\dots,k-1\) have \(k-1\) different birthdays, person \(k\) must avoid those \(k-1\) days, so the conditional probability of \(A_k\) is \((365-k+1)/365\). By Equation 2.1, \[
\Prob(\text{all different})=\frac{364}{365}\cdot\frac{363}{365}\cdots\frac{356}{365}\approx 0.883,
\] and two of the ten share a birthday with probability about \(0.117\).

Multiply out and the product is \(365\cdot364\cdots356/365^{10}\), exactly what counting ordered outcomes gives with Theorem 1.3. The chain rule and the counting are two readings of one fraction. I find the chain reading easier to set up, because you never have to decide what \(\Omega\) is. Seminar 1 (Problem 16) asks about 30 people. For them “all different” has probability about 0.294, so the probability that at least two share a birthday is about 0.706.
When an experiment happens in stages, draw it as a probability tree. Each branch carries the conditional probability of that step, given the path that leads to it. The probabilities on the branches leaving one node add up to 1 (that is Theorem 2.1). To get the probability of a whole path, multiply along it (the multiplication rule). To get the probability of an event, add the paths that make it up: different paths are mutually exclusive.

Example 2.3 (Two faulty bulbs in a row) A hypothetical lighting wholesaler in Kazan ships LED bulbs in boxes of 12. One box has 3 faulty bulbs in it. Oksana, a buyer, tests two bulbs from this box, one after the other, and does not put the first one back. Find the probability that

both bulbs are faulty;
exactly one is faulty.

Solution. Let \(F_1\) be “the first bulb is faulty” and \(F_2\) “the second bulb is faulty”. Figure 2.2 shows the tree. On the first draw, \(\Prob(F_1)=3/12\). If the first bulb was faulty, 11 bulbs are left and 2 of them are faulty, so \(\Prob(F_2\mid F_1)=2/11\). If the first was good, 3 of the remaining 11 are faulty, so \(\Prob(F_2\mid F_1^c)=3/11\).

\(\Prob(F_1\cap F_2)=\frac{3}{12}\cdot\frac{2}{11}=\frac{6}{132}=\frac{1}{22}\approx 0.045\).
Two paths: faulty then good, or good then faulty. \[
\frac{3}{12}\cdot\frac{9}{11}+\frac{9}{12}\cdot\frac{3}{11}=\frac{27}{132}+\frac{27}{132}=\frac{9}{22}\approx 0.409 .
\]

A check by counting, as in Example 1.7. Order does not matter, so there are \(\binom{12}{2}=66\) equally likely pairs. Both faulty: \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) pairs, \(3/66=1/22\). Exactly one faulty: \(3\cdot 9=27\) pairs, \(27/66=9/22\). Same answers.









Figure 2.2: Probability tree for Example 2.3. F = faulty, G = good. Branches carry conditional probabilities; the number at the end of a path is the product along it.





One more question about the same box: what is the probability that the second bulb is faulty, if we do not know anything about the first? Add the two paths that end in F: \[
\Prob(F_2)=\frac{3}{12}\cdot\frac{2}{11}+\frac{9}{12}\cdot\frac{3}{11}=\frac{6+27}{132}=\frac{1}{4}.
\] Exactly the same as for the first bulb, \(3/12\). Many people expect the second draw to be different because the box “has changed”, but it has changed in a way you do not know about. Summing over the branches like this is the law of total probability, which we meet properly in Section 2.4.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
2.3 Independence
Sometimes the extra information changes nothing at all: \(\Prob(A\mid B)=\Prob(A)\). A fair coin does not care what it showed last time.

Definition 2.2 (Independent events) Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if \[
\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\,\Prob(B).
\] If \(\Prob(B)>0\), this is the same as \(\Prob(A\mid B)=\Prob(A)\). If \(\Prob(A)>0\), it is the same as \(\Prob(B\mid A)=\Prob(B)\).

The equivalence is one line: divide \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B)\) by \(\Prob(B)\), and the left side becomes \(\Prob(A\mid B)\). We take the product form as the definition because it is symmetric in \(A\) and \(B\) and still makes sense when \(\Prob(B)=0\).
In the store of Example 1.3, \(\Prob(A)\Prob(B)=0.40\cdot0.55=0.22\), while \(\Prob(A\cap B)=0.20\). So promo code and app are not independent: app customers use promo codes a bit less often, 36% against 40% overall. Whether a gap like 0.22 against 0.20 is real or just noise in one day of orders is a question for module 3.
In practice independence is usually assumed, not computed. You assume it when there is a physical reason: two customers who do not know each other, two machines on separate power lines, two tosses of a coin. Be suspicious otherwise. Rain on Monday and rain on Tuesday are not independent, and neither are defaults of two firms in the same industry.
Students often mix up independent and mutually exclusive, because both sound like “the events have nothing to do with each other”. They are close to opposites. If \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, then \(\Prob(A\cap B)=0\) while \(\Prob(A)\Prob(B)>0\), so they are dependent: as soon as you learn that \(A\) happened, you know that \(B\) did not. A customer at a shop in Tula pays by card with probability 0.8 or in cash with probability 0.2, never both. Learning “paid by card” pushes the probability of cash from 0.2 down to 0. That is about as dependent as two events can be.

Theorem 2.3 (Complements of independent events) If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then so are \(A\) and \(B^c\), so are \(A^c\) and \(B\), and so are \(A^c\) and \(B^c\).


Proof. \(A\) is the union of the mutually exclusive events \(A\cap B\) and \(A\cap B^c\), so \[
\Prob(A\cap B^c)=\Prob(A)-\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)-\Prob(A)\Prob(B)=\Prob(A)\big(1-\Prob(B)\big)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B^c).
\] That is the first claim. Swap the roles of \(A\) and \(B\) to get the second. Apply the first claim to the independent pair \(A^c\) and \(B\) to get the third.

This is what makes “none of them” easy. If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, the probability that neither happens is \(\big(1-\Prob(A)\big)\big(1-\Prob(B)\big)\), and “at least one” is 1 minus that.
For more than two events we need the product rule for every sub-group of them, not only for pairs.

Definition 2.3 (Mutual independence) Events \(A_1,\dots,A_n\) are mutually independent if for every choice of two or more of them, the probability that all the chosen events occur is the product of their probabilities: \[
\Prob(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k})=\Prob(A_{i_1})\cdots\Prob(A_{i_k}).
\]

Repeated tosses of a coin and the answers of unrelated customers are the standard examples. Theorem 2.3 extends: replace any of the \(A_i\) by their complements and they stay mutually independent (we use this without proof). So if three suppliers are each late with probability 0.1, independently of each other, the probability that at least one of them is late is \(1-0.9^3=0.271\).
Asking for the product only for pairs is not enough. Toss a fair coin twice, and let \(A\) be “the first toss is heads”, \(B\) “the second toss is heads”, \(C\) “the two tosses agree”. Each has probability \(1/2\). Each pair meets only in the outcome HH, so each pairwise intersection has probability \(1/4=\frac12\cdot\frac12\), and the three events are pairwise independent. But \(A\cap B\cap C\) is again just HH, with probability \(1/4\), not \(1/8\). Knowing \(A\) and \(B\) tells you \(C\) for sure. In this course “independent” for several events always means mutually independent.

Example 2.4 (The gambler’s fallacy) A fair coin is tossed six times, and the tosses are mutually independent. Write H for heads and T for tails.

What is the probability of TTTTTT? Of HHHHHT?
What is the probability of exactly five heads and one tail, in any order?
The first five tosses were all tails. What is the probability that the sixth is heads?

Solution. (a) By Definition 2.3 each fixed sequence has probability \((1/2)^6=1/64\). Six tails in a row are exactly as likely as HHHHHT, or as any sequence that “looks random”. (b) The tail can be in any of six positions, so six sequences, each \(1/64\). They are mutually exclusive, so the answer is \(6/64=3/32\). (c) Let \(T_i\) be “toss \(i\) is tails” and \(H_6\) “toss 6 is heads”. Then \[
\Prob(H_6\mid T_1\cap\dots\cap T_5)=\frac{\Prob(T_1\cap\dots\cap T_5\cap H_6)}{\Prob(T_1\cap\dots\cap T_5)}=\frac{1/64}{1/32}=\frac12 .
\]

The coin has no memory. The belief that after five tails heads is “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy. Part of it comes from mixing up (a) and (b): “five heads and one tail” feels ordinary because it is a family of six sequences, and “six tails” feels special because it is a single one. Any single sequence, including HTHHTH, is as rare as six tails.
The same mistake happens in offices. A loan officer at a hypothetical bank in Novosibirsk approves 30% of small-business applications, and the applications in her queue come from unrelated firms, so treat them as independent. She has just rejected five in a row (probability \(0.7^5\approx 0.17\), not rare at all). Is the sixth applicant more likely to be approved? No, still 0.30. Like the coin, her queue has no memory.
Now the mirror image, which is where real life gets messier. If one firm has been turned down by five banks, the sixth bank’s decision is not a new toss of a coin. The five rejections tell you something about the application, and the sixth bank will probably reject it as well. Those events are not independent, because they share a cause. Bayes’ theorem, at the end of this lecture, is the tool for that kind of reasoning.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
2.4 Law of total probability
Lecture 1 promised that partitions would come back. Here they are. Often \(\Prob(A)\) is hard to see directly but easy within groups: we know the defect rate for each supplier, or the conversion rate for each customer segment. The law of total probability puts the groups back together.

Theorem 2.4 (Law of total probability) Let \(H_1,\dots,H_n\) be a partition of \(\Omega\) (Definition 1.3) with \(\Prob(H_i)>0\) for every \(i\). Then for every event \(A\) \[
\Prob(A)=\Prob(A\mid H_1)\Prob(H_1)+\dots+\Prob(A\mid H_n)\Prob(H_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n\Prob(A\mid H_i)\Prob(H_i).
\tag{2.2}\]


Proof. Exactly one of the \(H_i\) occurs, so \(A\) splits into the pieces \(A\cap H_1,\dots,A\cap H_n\). They are pairwise mutually exclusive, because the \(H_i\) are, and their union is \(A\). By axiom 3, \(\Prob(A)=\sum_i\Prob(A\cap H_i)\). By Theorem 2.2, \(\Prob(A\cap H_i)=\Prob(A\mid H_i)\Prob(H_i)\).

Two ways to picture it. On a tree, the first level is the partition \(H_1,\dots,H_n\) and the second level is “\(A\) or not \(A\)”. Then \(\Prob(A)\) is the sum over all paths that end in \(A\), which is what we did for the second bulb in Section 2.2. As a formula, \(\Prob(A)\) is a weighted average of the group rates \(\Prob(A\mid H_i)\), with the group sizes \(\Prob(H_i)\) as weights. A weighted average always lies between the smallest and the largest rate.

Example 2.5 (Phone cases from two factories) A hypothetical marketplace seller in Yekaterinburg sells phone cases. 60% of them come from a factory in Guangzhou and 40% from a workshop in Chelyabinsk. The Chelyabinsk cases cost 90 rubles more each, which is why the seller still buys mostly from Guangzhou. 3% of the Guangzhou cases are defective, and 1.5% of the Chelyabinsk ones. A customer receives a random case. What is the probability that it is defective?
Solution. Let \(H_1\) be “from Guangzhou”, \(H_2\) “from Chelyabinsk” (a partition), and \(D\) “defective”. By Equation 2.2, \[
\Prob(D)=0.03\cdot 0.60+0.015\cdot 0.40=0.018+0.006=0.024 .
\] So 2.4% of the cases are defective. That is between 1.5% and 3%, and closer to 3%, because Guangzhou supplies more.
In counts: out of 1000 cases, 600 come from Guangzhou and 18 of those are defective; 400 come from Chelyabinsk and 6 of those are defective. That makes 24 defective cases in 1000.


Example 2.6 (Conversion by customer segment) A hypothetical online school of English tracks visitors to its pricing page. 50% of them are new, 35% are returning and 15% were referred by a friend. The share who buy a course is 2% for new visitors, 8% for returning ones and 12% for referred ones.

What share of all visitors buy?
A referral campaign changes the mix to 35% new, 35% returning, 30% referred. The rate in each segment stays the same. What is the overall share now?

Solution. (a) The segments form a partition. By Equation 2.2, \[
\Prob(\text{buy})=0.02\cdot0.50+0.08\cdot0.35+0.12\cdot0.15=0.010+0.028+0.018=0.056 .
\] (b) The same rates with the new weights: \[
\Prob(\text{buy})=0.02\cdot0.35+0.08\cdot0.35+0.12\cdot0.30=0.007+0.028+0.036=0.071 .
\]

The overall conversion went from 5.6% to 7.1%, and not a single segment converts better than before. Only the mix changed. Keep this in mind whenever a dashboard shows one overall rate going up or down: first ask whether the rates moved or the mix did. Marketing teams like to report (b) as “the new landing page works”.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
2.5 Bayes’ theorem
The law of total probability goes forward, from the cause (which supplier, which segment) to the effect (a defect, a purchase). In practice we often see the effect and want the cause. This case is defective: which factory made it? This payment was flagged: is it fraud? Bayes’ theorem turns the conditioning around.

Theorem 2.5 (Bayes’ theorem) Let \(H_1,\dots,H_n\) be a partition of \(\Omega\) with \(\Prob(H_i)>0\) for every \(i\), and let \(A\) be an event with \(\Prob(A)>0\). Then for each \(k\) \[
\Prob(H_k\mid A)=\frac{\Prob(A\mid H_k)\Prob(H_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n\Prob(A\mid H_i)\Prob(H_i)}.
\tag{2.3}\] In particular, for two events with \(\Prob(A)>0\) and \(\Prob(B)>0\), \[
\Prob(B\mid A)=\frac{\Prob(A\mid B)\Prob(B)}{\Prob(A)}.
\]


Proof. By Definition 2.1, \(\Prob(H_k\mid A)=\Prob(H_k\cap A)/\Prob(A)\). The numerator is \(\Prob(A\mid H_k)\Prob(H_k)\) by Theorem 2.2, and the denominator is the sum in Equation 2.2. The two-event form is Theorem 2.2 written both ways, \(\Prob(A)\Prob(B\mid A)=\Prob(B)\Prob(A\mid B)\), divided by \(\Prob(A)\).

Two words go with the theorem. \(\Prob(H_k)\) is the prior probability of \(H_k\): what we believe before we see \(A\). \(\Prob(H_k\mid A)\) is the posterior probability: what we believe after. The numerator of Equation 2.3 is “how well \(H_k\) explains \(A\)” times the prior. The denominator is the same for every \(k\). It only makes the posteriors add up to 1.

Example 2.7 (Which factory made the defective case?) Continue Example 2.5. A customer sends back a defective case. What is the probability that it came from Guangzhou?
Solution. By Equation 2.3, \[
\Prob(H_1\mid D)=\frac{0.03\cdot0.60}{0.024}=\frac{0.018}{0.024}=0.75,\qquad \Prob(H_2\mid D)=\frac{0.006}{0.024}=0.25 .
\] The counts give the same thing in one glance: 18 of the 24 defective cases are from Guangzhou.

The prior for Guangzhou was 60%, and after seeing a defect it is 75%. A defect points towards Guangzhou, because defects are twice as common there. It is not proof: one defective case in four is from Chelyabinsk.
Gerd Gigerenzer and his co-authors put questions like the next one, about screening tests, to doctors, and most of the doctors in their studies got them wrong (Gigerenzer et al., 2007, Psychological Science in the Public Interest). Before you read the solution, write down your own guess.

Example 2.8 (Fraud alerts) A hypothetical bank processes 100,000 card payments a day, and 0.2% of them are fraudulent. Its fraud filter flags 99% of fraudulent payments, and it also flags 1% of legitimate ones by mistake. The vendor’s brochure calls this “99% accurate”. A payment has just been flagged. What is the probability that it is fraud?
Solution. Let \(F\) be “the payment is fraudulent” and \(L\) “the payment is flagged”. We know \(\Prob(F)=0.002\), \(\Prob(L\mid F)=0.99\) and \(\Prob(L\mid F^c)=0.01\). The partition is \(F\), \(F^c\). By Equation 2.3, \[
\Prob(F\mid L)=\frac{0.99\cdot0.002}{0.99\cdot0.002+0.01\cdot0.998}=\frac{0.00198}{0.00198+0.00998}=\frac{0.00198}{0.01196}\approx 0.166 .
\] Only about one flagged payment in six is fraud. Table 2.1 shows the same calculation in counts for one day.




Table 2.1: One day of payments in Example 2.8. Of the 1,196 flagged payments, 198 are fraud: \(198/1196\approx 0.166\).

Read the table row by row first. The filter flags 198 of the 200 frauds, which is the 99% from the brochure. But there are so many legitimate payments, 99,800, that 1% of them gives 998 false alarms, five times as many as the 198 real ones. The base rate, the share of all cases that really have the property (here 0.2% of payments are fraud), matters as much as the accuracy of the test. Whenever the thing you are looking for is rare, expect most alarms to be false, even from a good test.
That does not make the filter useless. The prior was 0.002 and the posterior is 0.166, more than 80 times higher. A flag is strong evidence, not a verdict. This is why the bank sends you an SMS to confirm a flagged payment instead of blocking your card.
And here is the swap from Example 2.1 once again. “99% accurate” describes \(\Prob(L\mid F)=0.99\). The question was about \(\Prob(F\mid L)\). People who answer “99%” have swapped the two. In court the same error is called the prosecutor’s fallacy: the court treats the probability of the evidence if the accused is innocent, \(\Prob(\text{evidence}\mid\text{innocent})\), as if it were the probability that the accused is innocent given the evidence, \(\Prob(\text{innocent}\mid\text{evidence})\). It appeared in the 1999 trial of Sally Clark in England, together with a worse mistake: the expert witness squared the probability of one sudden infant death to get the probability of two, as if the two deaths in one family were independent. Her conviction was overturned in 2003, mainly because of medical evidence that had not been disclosed.

title: 2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
text:
Exercises

Two dice are rolled and the sum is 8. What is the probability that at least one die shows a 3?
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(\Prob(A)=0.3\) and \(\Prob(B)=0.5\). Find \(\Prob(A\cup B)\) and the probability that neither occurs.
\(\Prob(A)=0.2\), \(\Prob(B)=0.3\), and \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive. Are they independent? One word, then one line of reason.
Priya runs a courier service. On 30% of days the weather is bad. On those days 20% of deliveries are late, on other days 5%. What is the probability that a random delivery is late? A delivery was late: what is the probability that the weather was bad that day?
Find the mistake. “An HR screening test is passed by 90% of strong candidates and by 20% of weak ones. 30% of applicants are strong. Ilya passed the test, so he is a strong candidate with probability 90%.”

Answers: (1) \(2/5\): the sum 8 comes from \((2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)\), and two of these contain a 3. (2) \(0.3+0.5-0.15=0.65\); neither: \(0.7\cdot0.5=0.35\). (3) No: \(\Prob(A\cap B)=0\) but \(\Prob(A)\Prob(B)=0.06\). (4) \(0.2\cdot0.3+0.05\cdot0.7=0.095\); \(0.06/0.095\approx 0.632\). (5) 90% is \(\Prob(\text{pass}\mid\text{strong})\), but the question asks for \(\Prob(\text{strong}\mid\text{pass})=0.27/(0.27+0.14)=0.27/0.41\approx 0.659\).

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.1 Random variables
Marat runs a small optician’s shop on Bauman Street in Kazan. On Saturday mornings he offers a free eye test, and this Saturday three customers have booked one. From experience, a customer orders glasses after the test with probability 0.4. The three don’t know each other, so each decides independently. A pair of glasses earns Marat 2,000 rubles, and each free test costs him 500 rubles in time and materials. (The coffee machine in the waiting room has been broken since October, which costs him nothing but some goodwill.)
Marat wants two numbers before Saturday. How many pairs should he expect to sell? And how far from that number does a typical Saturday land? Both questions are about one number we don’t know in advance: how many of the three customers order. A number like that is called a random variable.
Marat doesn’t care which customers order. He cares how many. The outcome of the morning is a list such as “first yes, second no, third yes”, and the thing he wants is a number computed from that list.
Figure 3.1: Marat’s Saturday as a tree. O = orders glasses (probability 0.4), N = does not (0.6). Each leaf shows the outcome, the value of \(X\) and the probability of that path.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
Definition 3.1 (Random variable) A random variable is a rule that gives a number to every outcome of an experiment. In the language of Lecture 1, it is a function from the sample space \(\Omega\) to the real numbers: each outcome gets exactly one number. We name random variables with capital letters: \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\).


Example 3.1 (Marat’s eight outcomes) Given: 3 customers; each one orders glasses (O) or does not (N). \(X\) is the number of customers who order.
Write an outcome as three letters, one per customer in the order they arrive: ONO means the first and third customers order and the second doesn’t. Each customer has 2 possibilities, so by the product rule (Theorem 1.3) there are \(2\cdot2\cdot2=8\) outcomes: \[
\Omega=\{\text{OOO},\ \text{OON},\ \text{ONO},\ \text{ONN},\ \text{NOO},\ \text{NON},\ \text{NNO},\ \text{NNN}\}.
\] \(X\) counts the letters O. So \(X(\text{OOO})=3\); \(X(\text{OON})=X(\text{ONO})=X(\text{NOO})=2\); \(X(\text{ONN})=X(\text{NON})=X(\text{NNO})=1\); \(X(\text{NNN})=0\). The possible values of \(X\) are \(0,1,2,3\). Figure 3.1 shows the same thing as a tree, drawn as in Lecture 2 (Figure 2.2). Three different mornings end with \(X=2\): \(X\) throws away the detail Marat doesn’t need.








NoteHow to read \(X\), \(x\) and \(\lbrace X=2\rbrace\)




\(X\) (capital, “big X”) is the random variable: the number of orders we will see on Saturday, not known yet.
\(x\) (small, “small x”) is a possible value of it: an ordinary number such as 0, 1, 2 or 3.
\(\{X=2\}\) is an event. Read it “the event that \(X\) equals 2”. It is the set of outcomes where \(X\) takes the value 2. For Marat, \(\{X=2\}=\{\text{OON},\text{ONO},\text{NOO}\}\), the three red leaves in Figure 3.1.
\(\{X\le 1\}\) reads “the event that \(X\) is at most 1”. For Marat, \(\{X\le1\}=\{X=0\}\cup\{X=1\}=\{\text{NNN},\text{ONN},\text{NON},\text{NNO}\}\).
\(\Prob(X=2)\) is short for \(\Prob(\{X=2\})\). We drop the curly brackets inside \(\Prob\).

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.2 The probability mass function

Definition 3.2 (Discrete random variable, PMF) A random variable \(X\) is discrete if its possible values can be listed: \(x_1, x_2, x_3,\dots\). The probability mass function (PMF) of \(X\) is \[
p(x)=\Prob(X=x),
\] for each value \(x\) of \(X\).

Marat’s \(X\) has four values, so it is discrete. In Lecture 4 we meet random variables that are not, such as a waiting time.






NoteHow to read \(p(x)\)



\(p(x)\) is read “p of x”. It is a function: a machine that takes a number \(x\) and gives back a probability. It is not \(p\) times \(x\). For Marat, \(p(2)\) (“p of two”) means \(\Prob(X=2)\), the probability that exactly two customers order. We’ll find in a moment that \(p(2)=0.288\). For a number that \(X\) never takes, the answer is zero: \(p(1.5)=\Prob(X=1.5)=0\), since nobody orders one and a half pairs.



Example 3.2 (Marat’s PMF) Given: 3 customers; each orders glasses with probability 0.4 and does not with probability 0.6; they decide independently. \(X\) is the number who order. Find the PMF of \(X\).
Solution. Take one path of the tree, say ONN. The customers are independent (Definition 2.3), so the probability of the path is the product along it: \(\Prob(\text{ONN})=0.4\cdot0.6\cdot0.6=0.144\). Do the same for every path (the leaves of Figure 3.1), then collect the paths by the value of \(X\). Different paths are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add.

\(X=0\): only NNN. \(p(0)=0.6\cdot0.6\cdot0.6=0.216\).
\(X=1\): ONN, NON, NNO, each \(0.4\cdot0.6\cdot0.6=0.144\). \(p(1)=3\cdot0.144=0.432\).
\(X=2\): OON, ONO, NOO, each \(0.4\cdot0.4\cdot0.6=0.096\). \(p(2)=3\cdot0.096=0.288\).
\(X=3\): only OOO. \(p(3)=0.4\cdot0.4\cdot0.4=0.064\).

\(p(x)=\Prob(X=x)\)

The four probabilities add up to \(0.216+0.432+0.288+0.064=1\). Figure 3.2 shows them as a bar chart.









Figure 3.2: PMF of Marat’s \(X\), the number of customers out of 3 who order glasses. The height of each bar is \(p(x)=\Prob(X=x)\).





The most likely value is 1, not 0. Each customer is more likely to say no than yes, but there is only one way to get three noes and three ways to get exactly one yes.






NoteHow to read the summation sign \(\sum\)



\(\sum\) is the Greek capital letter sigma, an S for “sum”. It means “add up”. You saw it in the law of total probability (Equation 2.2); now we read it properly. \[
\sum_{i=1}^{4} p(x_i)
\] reads “the sum of p of x i, for i from 1 to 4”. The letter \(i\) is the index, a counter. The number under the sign says where \(i\) starts, the number on top says where it stops. Put \(i=1\), then \(i=2\), \(i=3\), \(i=4\) into the expression and add the results.
\(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4\) (“x one, x two, …”) are the values of \(X\) in a list: \(x_1\) is the first value, \(x_2\) the second, and so on. The small number counts positions in the list; it is not the value itself. For Marat, \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=1\), \(x_3=2\), \(x_4=3\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{4} p(x_i)&=p(x_1)+p(x_2)+p(x_3)+p(x_4)\\
&=p(0)+p(1)+p(2)+p(3)\\
&=0.216+0.432+0.288+0.064=1.
\end{aligned}
\] When the sum runs over all values of \(X\), we often write just \(\sum_i\) and leave out the start and the stop.



Theorem 3.1 (Properties of a PMF) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with values \(x_1, x_2,\dots\) and PMF \(p\). Then

\(p(x_i)\ge 0\) for every \(i\);
\(\sum_i p(x_i)=1\).



Proof. 

Each \(p(x_i)\) is a probability, and probabilities are non-negative (axiom 1 of Definition 1.4).
Every outcome gives \(X\) exactly one value, so it lies in exactly one of the events \(\{X=x_1\}, \{X=x_2\},\dots\). These events are pairwise mutually exclusive and together make up \(\Omega\): they form a partition (Definition 1.3). By axioms 3 and 2, \[
\sum_i p(x_i)=\Prob(X=x_1)+\Prob(X=x_2)+\dots=\Prob(\Omega)=1.
\]


In practice Theorem 3.1 is a check: if your table does not add up to 1, a path is missing or counted twice.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.3 The cumulative distribution function

Definition 3.3 (Cumulative distribution function) The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a random variable \(X\) is \[
F(x)=\Prob(X\le x)
\] for every real number \(x\).

A note on letters. In Lecture 2 the letter \(F\) was an event (a faulty bulb, a fraudulent payment). From now on \(F\) is the CDF.






NoteHow to read \(F(x)\), \(\le\) and \(<\)



\(F(x)\) reads “F of x”. Like \(p(x)\), it is a function: put in a number, get a probability. \(F(1)=\Prob(X\le 1)\) reads “the probability that \(X\) is at most 1”.
\(\le\) reads “less than or equal to”, or “at most”. \(<\) reads “less than”, or “strictly less than”. For Marat:

\(X\le 1\) means \(X=0\) or \(X=1\), so \(\Prob(X\le1)=0.216+0.432=0.648\);
\(X<1\) means \(X=0\) only, so \(\Prob(X<1)=0.216\).

For a discrete random variable the two signs give different answers whenever the boundary (here 1) is a value \(X\) can take. “Cumulative” means “piling up”: \(F(x)\) adds the probabilities of all values from the left up to \(x\).



Example 3.3 (Marat’s CDF) Given: Marat’s PMF, \(p(0)=0.216\), \(p(1)=0.432\), \(p(2)=0.288\), \(p(3)=0.064\). Find \(F(x)\) for every \(x\), and in particular \(F(1.5)\).
Solution. Add the probabilities from the left: \(F(0)=0.216\); \(F(1)=0.216+0.432=0.648\); \(F(2)=0.648+0.288=0.936\); \(F(3)=0.936+0.064=1\).
Between the values nothing new is added. \(F(1.5)=\Prob(X\le1.5)\), and the values of \(X\) that are at most 1.5 are 0 and 1, so \(F(1.5)=0.216+0.432=0.648\), the same as \(F(1)\). Also \(F(-1)=0\), because \(X\) is never negative, and \(F(5)=1\), because \(X\) is always at most 5. In one formula: \[
F(x)=\begin{cases}
0, & x<0,\\
0.216, & 0\le x<1,\\
0.648, & 1\le x<2,\\
0.936, & 2\le x<3,\\
1, & x\ge 3.
\end{cases}
\]









Figure 3.3: CDF of Marat’s \(X\). It is flat between the values of \(X\) and jumps at 0, 1, 2 and 3 by \(p(x)\). At each jump the filled dot is the value of \(F\); the open dot is where the lower step ends. The dashed line reads off \(F(1.5)=0.648\).





Every discrete CDF is a staircase like this. It answers interval questions with one subtraction. If \(a<b\), the event \(\{X\le b\}\) splits into two mutually exclusive pieces, \(\{X\le a\}\) and \(\{a<X\le b\}\). So \(F(b)=F(a)+\Prob(a<X\le b)\), which gives \[
\Prob(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a).
\tag{3.1}\] For Marat (\(F(1)=0.648\), \(F(3)=1\)), the probability that 2 or 3 customers order is \(\Prob(1<X\le3)=F(3)-F(1)=1-0.648=0.352\). Check with the PMF: \(p(2)+p(3)=0.288+0.064=0.352\).
Watch the signs in Equation 3.1: \(<\) on the left, \(\le\) on the right. Students often use it for \(\Prob(1\le X\le 3)\) and get 0.352 again, but that event also contains \(X=1\). The correct answer is \(\Prob(1\le X\le3)=F(3)-F(0)=1-0.216=0.784\). With a discrete \(X\), always ask: is the boundary value included or not?

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.4 Expected value
Back to Marat’s first question: how many pairs should he expect to sell?

Definition 3.4 (Expected value) The expected value (also expectation or mean) of a discrete random variable \(X\) with values \(x_1,x_2,\dots\) and PMF \(p\) is \[
\E[X]=\sum_i x_i\,p(x_i).
\] We also write \(\mu\) for \(\E[X]\).







NoteHow to read \(\E[X]\) and \(\mu\)



\(\E[X]\) reads “E of X” or “the expected value of X”. The \(\E\) is not a number multiplied by \(X\): it is an operation done to \(X\), and the square brackets hold the random variable. \(\mu\) is the Greek letter mu (said “myoo”). In this course \(\mu\) is the mean of a random variable, \(\mu=\E[X]\).
In words, the formula says: multiply each value by its probability, then add. For Marat, written out with the four values: \[
\begin{aligned}
\E[X]&=0\cdot p(0)+1\cdot p(1)+2\cdot p(2)+3\cdot p(3)\\
&=0\cdot0.216+1\cdot0.432+2\cdot0.288+3\cdot0.064 .
\end{aligned}
\]



Example 3.4 (How many pairs Marat should expect) Given: Marat’s PMF, \(p(0)=0.216\), \(p(1)=0.432\), \(p(2)=0.288\), \(p(3)=0.064\).
Solution. \[
\E[X]=0\cdot0.216+1\cdot0.432+2\cdot0.288+3\cdot0.064=0+0.432+0.576+0.192=1.2 .
\] Marat should expect 1.2 pairs per Saturday morning.

A weighted average. The plain average of the values 0, 1, 2, 3 is 1.5. But 3 is rare (0.064) and 0 is common (0.216). The expected value weights each value by its probability, and the weights pull it down to 1.2.
A long-run average. Imagine 1,000 Saturdays like this one. About 216 of them end with no order, 432 with one, 288 with two and 64 with three. That is about \(0\cdot216+1\cdot432+2\cdot288+3\cdot64=1{,}200\) pairs, or 1.2 per Saturday.
“Expected” does not mean “most likely” (that is 1), and it does not mean “what will happen”. Marat will never sell 1.2 pairs. The expected value does not have to be a value \(X\) can take.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.5 Variance and standard deviation
Marat’s second question is how much the number of orders swings. First, one tool. We will want the expected value of things like \(X^2\). The rule is the same as for \(\E[X]\): compute the new quantity from each value of \(X\), weight it by the probability of that value, and add. For any function \(g\), \[
\E[g(X)]=\sum_i g(x_i)\,p(x_i).
\tag{3.2}\] The reason: \(g(X)\) is a new random variable, and it takes the value \(g(x_i)\) exactly when \(X=x_i\).






NoteHow to read squares, square roots and \(\sigma\)




\(X^2\) reads “X squared”: the random variable whose value is the square of the value of \(X\). If \(X=2\), then \(X^2=4\). By Equation 3.2, for Marat \(\E[X^2]=0^2\cdot0.216+1^2\cdot0.432+2^2\cdot0.288+3^2\cdot0.064\).
\((X-\mu)^2\) reads “X minus mu, all squared”. Brackets first, then square. It is the squared distance of \(X\) from its mean. For Marat with \(\mu=1.2\): if \(X=0\), then \((0-1.2)^2=(-1.2)^2=1.44\).
\(\sqrt{0.72}\) reads “the square root of 0.72”: the positive number whose square is 0.72. \(\sqrt{0.72}\approx0.85\) because \(0.85^2\approx0.72\).
\(\sigma\) is the small Greek letter sigma. It is the standard deviation, and \(\sigma^2\) (“sigma squared”) is the variance.
Units. \(X\) is in pairs of glasses, and so is \(X-\mu\). Then \((X-\mu)^2\) is in “pairs squared”, which means nothing to anyone. The square root brings us back to pairs.




Definition 3.5 (Variance and standard deviation) Let \(X\) have mean \(\mu=\E[X]\). The variance of \(X\) is \[
\Var(X)=\E\big[(X-\mu)^2\big]=\sum_i (x_i-\mu)^2\,p(x_i).
\] The standard deviation of \(X\) is \(\sigma=\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\Var(X)}\). So \(\Var(X)=\sigma^2\).

Why squares? The plain deviations \(X-\mu\) are positive above the mean and negative below it, and on average they cancel exactly: \(\sum_i(x_i-\mu)p(x_i)=\mu-\mu=0\). Squaring makes every deviation count, and big ones count much more.

Theorem 3.2 (Shortcut formula for the variance) \[
\Var(X)=\E[X^2]-\mu^2 .
\]

Proof
Expand the square: \((x_i-\mu)^2=x_i^2-2\mu x_i+\mu^2\). Then \[
\begin{aligned}
\Var(X)&=\sum_i x_i^2p(x_i)-2\mu\sum_i x_ip(x_i)+\mu^2\sum_i p(x_i)\\
&=\E[X^2]-2\mu\cdot\mu+\mu^2\cdot1=\E[X^2]-\mu^2,
\end{aligned}
\] using Equation 3.2, Definition 3.4 and Theorem 3.1.


Example 3.5 (How much Marat’s Saturdays swing) Given: Marat’s PMF, \(p(0)=0.216\), \(p(1)=0.432\), \(p(2)=0.288\), \(p(3)=0.064\), and mean \(\mu=1.2\). Find \(\Var(X)\) and \(\sigma\).
Solution by the definition. One row per value:

Solution by the shortcut. First \(\E[X^2]=0\cdot0.216+1\cdot0.432+4\cdot0.288+9\cdot0.064=0.432+1.152+0.576=2.16\), then \(\Var(X)=2.16-1.2^2=2.16-1.44=0.72\). Same answer, less work.
The standard deviation is \(\sigma=\sqrt{0.72}\approx0.85\) pairs: a typical Saturday lands around 0.85 pairs away from the mean of 1.2.

The most common mistake here: \(\E[X^2]\) is not \((\E[X])^2\). For Marat, \(\E[X^2]=2.16\) and \((\E[X])^2=1.44\). The gap between them is the variance, and it is never negative. If your variance comes out negative, you subtracted the wrong way round.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.6 Changing units: \(aX+b\)
Marat thinks in rubles, not pairs. Each pair earns 2,000 rubles, and the three free tests cost \(3\cdot500=1{,}500\) rubles whatever happens. His profit for the morning, in rubles, is \[
Y=2000X-1500 .
\]

Theorem 3.3 (Expectation and variance of \(aX+b\)) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be numbers. Then \[
\E[aX+b]=a\,\E[X]+b,\qquad \Var(aX+b)=a^2\Var(X),\qquad \operatorname{SD}(aX+b)=|a|\operatorname{SD}(X).
\]







NoteHow to read \(|a|\)



\(|a|\) reads “the absolute value of a”. It is \(a\) without its sign: \(|-3|=3\) and \(|3|=3\). In Lecture 2 the same bars around a set, \(|B|\), meant the number of its elements; around a number they mean the absolute value. So \(\operatorname{SD}(-X)=|-1|\cdot\operatorname{SD}(X)=\operatorname{SD}(X)\): a standard deviation is never negative.



Proof. For the expectation, use Equation 3.2 with \(g(x)=ax+b\): \[
\E[aX+b]=\sum_i(ax_i+b)p(x_i)=a\sum_i x_ip(x_i)+b\sum_i p(x_i)=a\,\E[X]+b\cdot1 .
\]

Proof
For the variance, write \(\mu=\E[X]\). The mean of \(aX+b\) is \(a\mu+b\), so the deviation of \(aX+b\) from its mean is \((aX+b)-(a\mu+b)=a(X-\mu)\). The \(b\) has gone. Square it: \(a^2(X-\mu)^2\). Take the expected value, using the first part with the number \(a^2\) in front: \(\Var(aX+b)=a^2\E[(X-\mu)^2]=a^2\Var(X)\). Take square roots for the SD: \(\sqrt{a^2}=|a|\).


Example 3.6 (Marat’s profit in rubles) Given: 2,000 rubles per pair, 3 free tests at 500 rubles each, so the profit is \(Y=2000X-1500\) rubles. From Example 3.4 and Example 3.5: \(\E[X]=1.2\), \(\Var(X)=0.72\), \(\operatorname{SD}(X)\approx0.85\). Find \(\E[Y]\), \(\Var(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{SD}(Y)\).
Solution. Here \(a=2000\) and \(b=-1500\). By Theorem 3.3, \[
\begin{aligned}
\E[Y]&=2000\cdot1.2-1500=2400-1500=900,\\
\Var(Y)&=2000^2\cdot0.72=4{,}000{,}000\cdot0.72=2{,}880{,}000,\\
\operatorname{SD}(Y)&=2000\cdot\sqrt{0.72}\approx 1{,}697 .
\end{aligned}
\] So the expected profit is 900 rubles and the standard deviation about 1,697 rubles. The variance is 2,880,000 “rubles squared”, a number nobody can picture: report the standard deviation. The swing is almost twice the mean, and about one Saturday in five (probability 0.216, no orders) is a loss of 1,500 rubles.

Two things go wrong here. First, \(b\) disappears from the variance. Paying 1,500 rubles for the tests shifts every profit down by the same amount, which moves the mean but not the spread. A popular wrong answer is \(\Var(Y)=2000\cdot0.72-1500\). Second, \(a\) is squared, so its sign disappears too: \(\Var(-X)=(-1)^2\Var(X)=\Var(X)\), never \(-\Var(X)\). Lecture 5 uses Theorem 3.3 for the normal distribution, so get it right now.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
3.7 Bernoulli and binomial distributions
Look at one of Marat’s customers alone: either they order or they don’t.

Definition 3.6 (Bernoulli distribution) A random variable \(X\) has the Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\), where \(0\le p\le1\), if it takes only two values: \[
\Prob(X=1)=p,\qquad \Prob(X=0)=1-p .
\] The value 1 is called a success and 0 a failure.

A parameter is a number that picks one member of a family of distributions: Bernoulli(0.4) and Bernoulli(0.9) are two members of one family. “Success” is just a label for what we count, even when it is something bad, such as a default.
The mean and variance take two lines. With values 0 and 1, \[
\E[X]=0\cdot(1-p)+1\cdot p=p,\qquad \E[X^2]=0^2\cdot(1-p)+1^2\cdot p=p,
\] so by Theorem 3.2, \(\Var(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)\). One of Marat’s customers is Bernoulli(0.4): mean 0.4, variance \(0.4\cdot0.6=0.24\).

Definition 3.7 (Binomial distribution) Repeat a trial \(n\) times, where

the number of trials \(n\) is fixed in advance;
each trial ends in success or failure;
every trial has the same probability of success \(p\);
the trials are independent.

Let \(X\) be the number of successes. Then \(X\) has the binomial distribution with parameters \(n\) and \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), and \[
\Prob(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n .
\tag{3.3}\]







NoteHow to read \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) and \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\)



The sign \(\sim\) (“tilde”) reads “has the distribution”. \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,\,0.4)\) reads “X has the binomial distribution with \(n=3\) and \(p=0.4\)”. That is Marat’s \(X\): 3 customers, success = an order, \(p=0.4\). A Bernoulli(\(p\)) variable is \(\operatorname{Bin}(1,p)\).
In Equation 3.3, \(k\) is a placeholder for “how many successes we ask about”. \(p^k\) means \(p\) multiplied by itself \(k\) times, and any number to the power 0 is 1. For Marat and \(k=1\): \[
p^1(1-p)^{3-1}=0.4^1\cdot0.6^2=0.4\cdot0.36=0.144,
\] the probability of one particular path with one order, such as ONN. Then \(\binom{3}{1}=3\) counts those paths (ONN, NON, NNO), and \(\Prob(X=1)=3\cdot0.144=0.432\).


Why does Equation 3.3 hold in general? A sequence of \(n\) trials with exactly \(k\) successes and \(n-k\) failures has probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\), by independence (Definition 2.3). The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose the \(k\) positions of the successes, \(\binom nk\) (Definition 1.8, Equation 1.2). Different sequences are mutually exclusive, so we add \(\binom nk\) equal probabilities. Check with Marat and \(k=2\): \(\binom32\cdot0.4^2\cdot0.6=3\cdot0.16\cdot0.6=0.288\), as in Example 3.2.

Theorem 3.4 (Mean and variance of the binomial distribution) If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), then \[
\E[X]=np,\qquad \Var(X)=np(1-p).
\]

Proof
Idea. Let \(X_j=1\) if trial \(j\) is a success and \(X_j=0\) if not. Each \(X_j\) is Bernoulli(\(p\)), and \(X=X_1+X_2+\dots+X_n\) counts the successes. In Lecture 6 we prove that the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, so \(\E[X]=p+p+\dots+p=np\). For independent random variables the same holds for variances, so \(\Var(X)=n\cdot p(1-p)\).

For Marat, \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,\,0.4)\): \(\E[X]=3\cdot0.4=1.2\) and \(\Var(X)=3\cdot0.4\cdot0.6=0.72\), as in Example 3.4 and Example 3.5.

title: 3  Discrete random variables
text:
Exercises

A guesthouse in Suzdal gets \(X\) late cancellations per weekend, with \(\Prob(X=0)=0.5\), \(\Prob(X=1)=0.3\) and \(\Prob(X=2)=c\), and no other values. Find \(c\), \(F(1.5)\), \(\Prob(X<1)\), \(\E[X]\) and \(\Var(X)\).
The daily number of customers \(W\) of a food truck has \(\E[W]=50\) and \(\Var(W)=16\). Each customer pays 300 rubles, and the spot costs 4,000 rubles a day, so the daily profit is \(300W-4000\) rubles. Find its expected value and standard deviation. What is \(\Var(-W)\)?
Binomial or not? One word each, then one line of reason. (a) The number of heads in 6 tosses of a fair coin. (b) The number of faulty bulbs among 2 bulbs taken without putting back from a box of 12 that has 3 faulty ones. (c) The number of customers Marat tests until the first one orders.
Each of 5 visitors to a car showroom in Kaliningrad books a test drive with probability 0.2, independently of the others. Let \(X\) be the number who book. Find \(\Prob(X=2)\), \(\Prob(X\ge1)\), \(\E[X]\) and \(\Var(X)\).

Answers: (1) \(c=1-0.5-0.3=0.2\); \(F(1.5)=0.5+0.3=0.8\); \(\Prob(X<1)=\Prob(X=0)=0.5\); \(\E[X]=0.3+2\cdot0.2=0.7\); \(\E[X^2]=0.3+4\cdot0.2=1.1\), so \(\Var(X)=1.1-0.49=0.61\). (2) \(300\cdot50-4000=11{,}000\) rubles; \(\operatorname{SD}=300\cdot\sqrt{16}=1{,}200\) rubles; \(\Var(-W)=16\). (3) (a) Yes, \(\operatorname{Bin}(6,\,0.5)\). (b) No: after the first draw \(p\) changes to \(2/11\) or \(3/11\) (Lecture 2), so the trials are not independent. (c) No: the number of trials is not fixed (geometric distribution, Lecture 4). (4) \(\binom52\cdot0.2^2\cdot0.8^3=10\cdot0.04\cdot0.512=0.2048\); \(1-0.8^5=1-0.32768\approx0.672\); \(\E[X]=5\cdot0.2=1\); \(\Var(X)=5\cdot0.2\cdot0.8=0.8\). The full practice is in Seminar 3.

text:
Problem 1
A café chain surveys one random customer. Let \(A\) be “ordered coffee” and \(B\) “ordered a dessert”. Write each statement as an expression in \(A\), \(B\) and the set operations:

coffee and no dessert;
neither coffee nor dessert;
at least one of the two;
exactly one of the two.







NoteSolution




\(A\cap B^c\).
\(A^c\cap B^c\), which equals \((A\cup B)^c\) by Theorem 1.1.
\(A\cup B\).
Either coffee without dessert or dessert without coffee: \((A\cap B^c)\cup(A^c\cap B)\). These two pieces are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add. Do not write \(A\cup B\) here: it also contains “both”.

Each answer is the shaded region in the matching panel of the picture.

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 2
If time allows.
Every Monday a sushi bar in Vladivostok gets fish, rice and vegetables from three different suppliers. The chef only really worries about the fish. Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be the events that the fish, the rice and the vegetables arrive on time. Write as expressions in \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\):

all three deliveries are on time;
none is on time;
exactly one is on time;
at least two are on time;
not all three are on time.

Then use De Morgan’s laws to write (b) and (e) in a second way. Are (b) and (e) the same event?






NoteSolution




\(A\cap B\cap C\).
\(A^c\cap B^c\cap C^c\).
Three mutually exclusive pieces, one for each supplier who is on time: \((A\cap B^c\cap C^c)\cup(A^c\cap B\cap C^c)\cup(A^c\cap B^c\cap C)\).
\((A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)\cup(B\cap C)\). This union contains “all three on time” too, which is right: three is at least two. The picture shades (c) and (d).











\((A\cap B\cap C)^c\).

De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 1.1) work for three events with the same sentence: an outcome is outside \(A\cup B\cup C\) exactly when it is outside each of the three. So (b) is \((A\cup B\cup C)^c\), “not even one on time”, and (e) is \(A^c\cup B^c\cup C^c\), “at least one is late”.
They are not the same event. In (b) every delivery is late, while (e) needs only one late delivery. A Monday when only the fish is late is in (e) and not in (b).

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 3
At an online store, \(\Prob(A)=0.62\) for “the order contains a discounted item”, \(\Prob(B)=0.35\) for “the order is paid in instalments”, and \(\Prob(A\cup B)=0.78\). Find

\(\Prob(A\cap B)\);
the probability of an order with neither;
the probability of an order with exactly one of the two.







NoteSolution




From Theorem 1.2(4), \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cup B)=0.62+0.35-0.78=0.19\).
\(1-\Prob(A\cup B)=0.22\).
Exactly one is the union minus the overlap: \(0.78-0.19=0.59\). Check by pieces: discount only \(0.62-0.19=0.43\), instalments only \(0.35-0.19=0.16\), and \(0.43+0.16=0.59\).


p_discount, p_instalment, p_either = 0.62, 0.35, 0.78
p_both = p_discount + p_instalment - p_either
print(f"P(both) = {p_both:.2f}")
print(f"P(neither) = {1 - p_either:.2f}")
print(f"P(exactly one) = {p_either - p_both:.2f}")

P(both) = 0.19
P(neither) = 0.22
P(exactly one) = 0.59

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 4
Two short proofs, then a use for them. In (a) and (b) use only the axioms of probability and their consequences from Lecture 1.

Show that \(\Prob(A\cap B^c)=\Prob(A)-\Prob(A\cap B)\). The event \(A\cap B^c\), “\(A\) but not \(B\)”, is written \(A\setminus B\) in many books.
Show that \(\Prob(A\cap B)\ge\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)-1\).
At a regional bank in Yekaterinburg, 80% of the clients use the mobile app and 70% get their salary on the bank’s card. At least what share of the clients do both? What is the largest possible share? For each of the two extremes, describe in one sentence what the client base looks like.
Can two mutually exclusive events have probabilities 0.7 and 0.5? One word, then a reason in one line.







NoteSolution




An outcome in \(A\) is either in \(B\) or not, so \(A\) splits into two mutually exclusive pieces, \(A\cap B\) and \(A\cap B^c\). By axiom 3 of Definition 1.4, \(\Prob(A)=\Prob(A\cap B)+\Prob(A\cap B^c)\). Move \(\Prob(A\cap B)\) to the other side.
By Theorem 1.2(4), \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cup B)\). By Theorem 1.2(3), \(\Prob(A\cup B)\le1\), so we subtract at most 1.
Let \(A\) be “uses the app” and \(B\) “has a salary card”. By (b), \(\Prob(A\cap B)\ge0.80+0.70-1=0.50\). The share is exactly 0.50 when \(\Prob(A\cup B)=1\): every client has at least one of the two, so the 20% without the app all have a salary card and the 30% without a salary card all use the app.

For the largest share: \(A\cap B\subseteq B\), so by Theorem 1.2(3) it is at most \(\Prob(B)=0.70\). It equals 0.70 when every salary-card client also uses the app. Without data on the overlap, the bank can only say that between 50% and 70% of its clients do both.

No. Mutually exclusive means \(\Prob(A\cap B)=0\), while (b) gives \(\Prob(A\cap B)\ge0.7+0.5-1=0.2\). Put differently, \(\Prob(A\cup B)\) would be \(1.2\), and no probability exceeds 1.


p_app, p_card = 0.80, 0.70
lowest = max(0, p_app + p_card - 1)
highest = min(p_app, p_card)
print(f"share with both: between {lowest:.2f} and {highest:.2f}")

share with both: between 0.50 and 0.70

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 5
Find the mistake in this solution.

Two dice are rolled. The possible sums are 2, 3, …, 12, that is 11 values. So the probability that the sum is 7 is \(1/11\).

Give the correct answer, and also the probability that the sum is 2.






NoteSolution



The 11 sums are not equally likely, so Definition 1.5 does not apply to them. The equally likely outcomes are the 36 ordered pairs. Six pairs give 7, so \(\Prob(\text{sum}=7)=6/36=1/6\approx 0.167\), while only \((1,1)\) gives 2, so \(\Prob(\text{sum}=2)=1/36\approx 0.028\). The claimed \(1/11\approx 0.091\) is wrong for both.

from itertools import product
from collections import Counter

sums = Counter(i + j for i, j in product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
for total in (2, 7, 12):
    n_ways = sums[total]
    print(f"P(sum = {total}) = {n_ways}/36 = {n_ways / 36:.3f}")

P(sum = 2) = 1/36 = 0.028
P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 0.167
P(sum = 12) = 1/36 = 0.028
