title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 6
A small supermarket in Yaroslavl has four cashiers open. Three customers reach the tills at the same moment, and each picks a cashier at random: all four are equally likely, whatever the other two customers chose.

How many equally likely outcomes are there? Describe one outcome in words.
Find the probability that all three go to different cashiers, that all three go to the same cashier, and that exactly two of them share a cashier.
Rustam, a classmate, says: “There are only three patterns: all at one cashier, two at one and one at another, all at different cashiers. So each pattern has probability 1/3.” Find his mistake.







NoteSolution




An outcome records which cashier each customer picks, in order: customer 1, customer 2, customer 3. For example, \((2,2,4)\) means the first two go to cashier 2 and the third to cashier 4. Three stages with 4 choices each (Theorem 1.3) give \(|\Omega|=4^3=64\) ordered triples, all equally likely.
All different: the three customers take an arrangement of 3 cashiers out of 4 (Definition 1.7), \(4\cdot3\cdot2=24\) outcomes, so \(\Prob=24/64=0.375\).

All at the same cashier: 4 outcomes, one for each cashier, so \(\Prob=4/64=0.0625\).
Exactly two share: what is left, \(64-24-4=36\) outcomes, so \(\Prob=36/64=0.5625\). A direct count agrees: choose the two customers who share (\(\binom32=3\) ways), their cashier (4 ways) and the third customer’s cashier (3 ways), which gives \(3\cdot4\cdot3=36\).

The three patterns are a coarse sample space, the trap from Experiments and outcomes and the same one as the eleven sums in Problem 5. They are not equally likely: they contain 4, 36 and 24 of the 64 outcomes. Definition 1.5 needs equally likely outcomes, and only the 64 ordered triples are.


from itertools import product
from collections import Counter

# one outcome = (cashier of customer 1, of customer 2, of customer 3)
outcomes = list(product(range(1, 5), repeat=3))
n_used = Counter(len(set(choice)) for choice in outcomes)
names = {3: "all different", 1: "all the same",
         2: "exactly two share"}
for used, name in names.items():
    share = n_used[used] / len(outcomes)
    print(f"P({name}) = {n_used[used]}/{len(outcomes)} = {share:.4f}")

P(all different) = 24/64 = 0.3750
P(all the same) = 4/64 = 0.0625
P(exactly two share) = 36/64 = 0.5625

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 7
Does order matter? For each situation say whether you count permutations, arrangements, combinations, or ordered choices with repetition (the product rule). Then count.

Six start-ups pitch at a demo day in Skolkovo. In how many orders can they go on stage?
A student club has 15 members. In how many ways can it elect a chair, a deputy and a treasurer (three different people)?
The same club sends 3 of its 15 members to a conference in Saint Petersburg. How many different delegations are possible?
A coffee shop prints a code of 3 capital Latin letters on each loyalty card, and letters may repeat (AAB is allowed). How many codes are there?







NoteSolution



Use the swap test: swap two chosen items and see whether the outcome changes.

All six go in a row and order matters: a permutation (Definition 1.6), \(6!=720\).
Swap the chair and the treasurer and you get a different board, so order matters, and nobody holds two posts: an arrangement of 3 from 15 (Definition 1.7), \(15\cdot14\cdot13=2730\).
Swap two delegates and the delegation is the same group: a combination (Definition 1.8), \(\binom{15}{3}=455\). Check with Theorem 1.4: \(2730/3!=455\), because each delegation can share out the three posts of (b) in \(3!=6\) ways.
Order matters (ABA is not AAB) and letters may repeat: three stages with 26 choices each (Theorem 1.3), \(26^3=17\,576\).


from math import factorial, perm, comb

print(f"(a) pitch orders: {factorial(6)}")
print(f"(b) chair, deputy, treasurer: {perm(15, 3)}")
print(f"(c) delegations: {comb(15, 3)}")
print(f"    check: 2730 / 3! = {perm(15, 3) // factorial(3)}")
print(f"(d) loyalty codes: {26 ** 3:,}")

(a) pitch orders: 720
(b) chair, deputy, treasurer: 2730
(c) delegations: 455
    check: 2730 / 3! = 455
(d) loyalty codes: 17,576

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 8
A Wi-Fi password has 8 characters. Each character is a lowercase Latin letter (26 options) or a digit (10 options).

How many passwords are possible?
How many contain at least one digit?
A password is generated at random: each character is one of the 36 symbols, all equally likely, chosen without looking at the others. What is the probability that it contains no digit?







NoteSolution




Eight stages with 36 choices each (Theorem 1.3): \(36^8=2\,821\,109\,907\,456\).
“At least one” is a job for the complement. Passwords with no digit use only letters: \(26^8=208\,827\,064\,576\). So \(36^8-26^8=2\,612\,282\,842\,880\).
\(26^8/36^8=(26/36)^8\approx 0.074\).


n_all = 36 ** 8
n_letters_only = 26 ** 8
print(f"all passwords: {n_all:,}")
print(f"with at least one digit: {n_all - n_letters_only:,}")
print(f"P(no digit) = {n_letters_only / n_all:.3f}")

all passwords: 2,821,109,907,456
with at least one digit: 2,612,282,842,880
P(no digit) = 0.074

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 9
If time allows.
A bakery near Chistye Prudy in Moscow puts 8 cakes in a row in its window: 3 Napoleons, 3 medoviks (Russian honey cakes) and 2 cheesecakes. Cakes of one kind look exactly the same. How many different-looking rows can the window have? Count it in two ways.






NoteSolution



First way. If all 8 cakes were different, there would be \(8!=40\,320\) rows (Definition 1.6). But swapping the three Napoleons among themselves does not change how the window looks, and the same holds for the medoviks and the cheesecakes. So each look is counted \(3!\cdot3!\cdot2!=72\) times, the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.4, part 3: \[
\frac{8!}{3!\,3!\,2!}=\frac{40\,320}{72}=560 .
\]
Second way. A look is fixed once we know which places hold which kind. Choose the 3 places for the Napoleons out of 8: \(\binom83=56\). Then the 3 places for the medoviks out of the 5 left: \(\binom53=10\). The cheesecakes take the last 2 places. By Theorem 1.3, \(56\cdot10=560\).

from itertools import permutations
from math import comb

window = "NNNMMMCC"   # N = Napoleon, M = medovik, C = cheesecake
n_looks = len(set(permutations(window)))
print(f"different-looking rows: {n_looks}")
print(f"second way: C(8,3) * C(5,3) = {comb(8, 3) * comb(5, 3)}")

different-looking rows: 560
second way: C(8,3) * C(5,3) = 560

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 10
A shelf has 20 packs of yoghurt and 3 are expired. An inspector takes 4 packs at random. Example 1.7 gave the probabilities for one batch. Now a second shelf has 40 packs, 6 of them expired (the same 15%). The inspector again takes 4. Is the probability of finding no expired pack larger, smaller or about equal? Guess first, then compute.






NoteSolution



Number of ways to take 4 packs with none expired, over all ways: \[
\frac{\binom{34}{4}}{\binom{40}{4}}=\frac{46\,376}{91\,390}\approx 0.507.
\] For the first shelf it was \(0.491\). A bigger shelf with the same share of bad packs makes it slightly easier to miss them, because taking one pack changes the remaining share less. The difference is small.

from scipy import stats

# stats.hypergeom(M=total packs, n=expired packs, N=packs taken)
for total, expired in [(20, 3), (40, 6)]:
    p_none = stats.hypergeom(total, expired, 4).pmf(0)
    print(f"{total} packs, {expired} expired: P(none) = {p_none:.3f}")

20 packs, 3 expired: P(none) = 0.491
40 packs, 6 expired: P(none) = 0.507

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 11
A sales department has 7 managers and 5 analysts. Five people are chosen at random for a trade fair. What is the probability that the group has at least 2 analysts?






NoteSolution



Order does not matter, so \(|\Omega|=\binom{12}{5}=792\). “At least 2 analysts” means 2, 3, 4 or 5, which is four cases. The complement has only two: 0 or 1 analyst.

0 analysts: \(\binom{5}{0}\binom{7}{5}=21\).
1 analyst: \(\binom{5}{1}\binom{7}{4}=5\cdot35=175\).

So \(\Prob=1-\dfrac{21+175}{792}=\dfrac{596}{792}\approx 0.753\).

from math import comb

n_groups = comb(12, 5)
n_few_analysts = sum(comb(5, k) * comb(7, 5 - k) for k in (0, 1))
print(f"P(at least 2 analysts) = {1 - n_few_analysts / n_groups:.3f}")

P(at least 2 analysts) = 0.753

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 12
The shuttle from Rumyantsevo metro station to a business park leaves every 12 minutes. Lena comes to the stop at a random moment, without looking at the timetable.

What is the probability that she waits more than 5 minutes?
What is the probability that she waits exactly 5 minutes? Is this event impossible?







NoteSolution




Look at one 12-minute gap between two departures. Lena’s arrival is a uniform point in it (Definition 1.9). She waits more than 5 minutes if she arrives in the first 7 minutes after a departure (the blue part of the picture), so \(\Prob=7/12\approx0.583\). As in Example 1.8, it is a length divided by a length.











Waiting exactly 5 minutes means arriving at one single moment, an interval of length 0, so the probability is 0. The event is not impossible: Lena arrives at some moment, and every single moment has probability 0 (the remark at the end of Geometric probability).


import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
# arrival = minutes after the last departure
arrival = rng.uniform(0, 12, 1_000_000)
wait = 12 - arrival
p_sim = np.mean(wait > 5)
print(f"simulated P(wait > 5) = {p_sim:.3f}, exact = {7 / 12:.3f}")
print(f"simulated P(wait exactly 5) = {np.mean(wait == 5):.3f}")

simulated P(wait > 5) = 0.584, exact = 0.583
simulated P(wait exactly 5) = 0.000

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 13
Priya and Kemal agree to meet at a bus stop between 18:00 and 19:00. Each arrives at a random moment of that hour, independently, and waits 10 minutes. What is the probability that they meet? Draw the region.






NoteSolution



As in Example 1.9, \((x,y)\) is uniform in the square \([0,60]^2\) and they meet when \(|x-y|\le10\), the shaded band in the picture. The two corner triangles outside the band have legs \(60-10=50\), so together they have area \(50^2\). Then \[
\Prob(\text{meet})=1-\Big(\frac{50}{60}\Big)^2=\frac{11}{36}\approx 0.306.
\]










import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_trials = 1_000_000
arrive_priya = rng.uniform(0, 60, n_trials)
arrive_kemal = rng.uniform(0, 60, n_trials)
p_meet = np.mean(np.abs(arrive_priya - arrive_kemal) <= 10)
print(f"simulated P(meet) = {p_meet:.3f}, exact = {11 / 36:.3f}")

simulated P(meet) = 0.305, exact = 0.306

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 14
A warehouse near Podolsk has one loading dock. Two trucks are due between 8:00 and 9:00. Each arrives at a random moment of that hour, and the moment one truck arrives has nothing to do with when the other one does. Truck 1 needs the dock for 10 minutes, truck 2 for 20 minutes. If a truck arrives while the other one is unloading, it has to wait, and Anvar, the dispatcher, calls that a clash. An unloading that runs past 9:00 is fine, because the dock is open until noon.

Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the arrival times of truck 1 and truck 2 in minutes after 8:00. Write the condition “no clash” in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).
Find the probability of a clash. Draw the square and shade the clash region.
The shaded band is not symmetric around the diagonal \(y=x\). Why not? Compare with the case where each truck needs 15 minutes.







NoteSolution




Truck 1 uses the dock from \(x\) to \(x+10\) and truck 2 from \(y\) to \(y+20\). No clash means that one truck is done before the other arrives: either \(y\ge x+10\) (truck 1 came first and finished) or \(x\ge y+20\) (truck 2 came first and finished).
The point \((x,y)\) is uniform in the square \([0,60]^2\) of area 3600 (Definition 1.9). The region \(y\ge x+10\) is the triangle above the line \(y=x+10\), with legs \(60-10=50\) and area \(50^2/2=1250\). The region \(x\ge y+20\) is the triangle below the line \(y=x-20\), with legs \(60-20=40\) and area \(40^2/2=800\). These are the two white corners in the picture below. So \[
\Prob(\text{clash})=1-\frac{1250+800}{3600}=\frac{1550}{3600}=\frac{31}{72}\approx 0.431 .
\]
The clash band runs from the line \(y=x-20\) up to the line \(y=x+10\). Above the diagonal truck 1 came first, and truck 2 clashes if it arrives within 10 minutes, the time truck 1 needs. Below the diagonal truck 2 came first, and the dangerous stretch is 20 minutes long. So each side of the band is as wide as the unloading time of the truck that came first. If each truck needed 15 minutes, the band would be \(|x-y|<15\), centred on the diagonal, the same region as in Example 1.9, and \(\Prob(\text{clash})=7/16\approx0.438\). In both cases the trucks need 30 minutes in total, and the two answers are close but not equal.











import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_trials = 1_000_000
truck_1 = rng.uniform(0, 60, n_trials)
truck_2 = rng.uniform(0, 60, n_trials)
no_clash = (truck_2 >= truck_1 + 10) | (truck_1 >= truck_2 + 20)
p_clash = 1 - np.mean(no_clash)
print(f"simulated P(clash) = {p_clash:.3f}, exact = {31 / 72:.3f}")

simulated P(clash) = 0.430, exact = 0.431

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 15
If time allows.
A warehouse floor is an \(8\times8\) grid of squares. Two robots, one white and one black, are put on two different squares chosen at random. They “see each other” if they stand in the same row or in the same column. What is the probability that they do not see each other?






NoteSolution



Treat the placements as ordered, because the robots have different colours: \(64\cdot63\) equally likely outcomes. Fix the white robot’s square (64 ways). The black robot must be outside its row and column, which leaves \(64-8-8+1=49\) squares, the blue ones in the picture (the white robot’s own square was subtracted twice). So \[
\Prob=\frac{64\cdot 49}{64\cdot 63}=\frac{49}{63}=\frac79\approx 0.778.
\] A common wrong answer is \(49/64\), which forgets that the black robot cannot take the same square as the white one.










from itertools import permutations

squares = [(row, col) for row in range(8) for col in range(8)]
n_safe = sum(1 for a, b in permutations(squares, 2)
             if a[0] != b[0] and a[1] != b[1])
n_all = 64 * 63
print(f"P(no sight line) = {n_safe}/{n_all} = {n_safe / n_all:.3f}")

P(no sight line) = 3136/4032 = 0.778

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 16
If time allows.
In a team of 30 employees, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday? Ignore 29 February and assume all 365 days are equally likely.






NoteSolution



Count the opposite: all 30 birthdays are different. Ordered, with \(365^{30}\) equally likely outcomes, the favourable ones are \(365\cdot364\cdots336\). So \[
\Prob(\text{some pair shares})=1-\frac{365\cdot364\cdots336}{365^{30}}\approx 0.706.
\] Already 23 people give more than 50% (see the picture). When I ask a group to guess, the guesses are usually far lower, because they compare their own birthday against 29 others, while the question allows any of the \(\binom{30}{2}=435\) pairs.










import numpy as np

n_people = 30
p_all_different = np.prod([(365 - i) / 365 for i in range(n_people)])
print(f"exact: P(shared birthday) = {1 - p_all_different:.3f}")

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
birthdays = rng.integers(0, 365, size=(100_000, n_people))
has_match = [len(set(row)) < n_people for row in birthdays]
print(f"simulation: {np.mean(has_match):.3f}")

exact: P(shared birthday) = 0.706
simulation: 0.708

title: Seminar 1: events, counting, classical and geometric probability
text:
Problem 17*
This problem goes past Lecture 1 and is not examinable.
An ice-cream kiosk in Gorky Park sells cups of 3 scoops. There are 5 flavours, and a flavour may be repeated: three scoops of pistachio is a perfectly good cup. The order of the scoops in the cup does not matter. How many different cups can Sofia, who runs the kiosk, list on her menu board?
None of the formulas from the lecture fits directly. Sort the cups by type: all three scoops the same, two the same and one different, all three different.






NoteSolution



All three the same: choose the flavour, 5 cups.
Two the same and one different: choose the flavour that appears twice (5 ways), then the single flavour from the other 4 (4 ways), \(5\cdot4=20\) cups by Theorem 1.3. Here the two choices play different roles, since two vanilla and one mango is not the same cup as two mango and one vanilla.
All three different: a set of 3 flavours from 5, \(\binom53=10\) cups (Definition 1.8).
The three types do not overlap, so there are \(5+20+10=35\) cups. Other books give a shortcut for unordered choices with repetition, \(k\) items from \(n\) kinds: \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\). Here it is \(\binom{7}{3}=35\).

from itertools import combinations_with_replacement

flavours = ["vanilla", "chocolate", "pistachio", "mango",
            "salted caramel"]
cups = list(combinations_with_replacement(flavours, 3))
print(f"different cups: {len(cups)}")
print("the first three:")
for cup in cups[:3]:
    print("  ", ", ".join(cup))

different cups: 35
the first three:
   vanilla, vanilla, vanilla
   vanilla, vanilla, chocolate
   vanilla, vanilla, pistachio

Problem 1
Material from Lecture 2 (2  Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem). The firms on this sheet are made up, and so are their numbers. The short drills in Problems 1, 3 and 4 and parts 3(c) and 5(d) are marked if time allows. The starred Problem 9* goes past the lecture and is not examinable: it is for a strong group or for homework. As in Seminar 1, work by hand first and let the Python check you.
Short drill, if time allows.
HR at an IT outsourcing firm in Nizhny Novgorod asked all 504 employees two questions: do you work mostly from home or from the office, and are you satisfied with your job? Four people did not answer and are left out. The other 500 answers are in the table.
One of the 500 is picked at random. Let \(S\) be “satisfied” and \(R\) “works remotely”.

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Satisfied
Not satisfied
Total




Remote
168
42
210


Office
174
116
290


Total
342

500





Find \(\Prob(S\mid R)\) and \(\Prob(R\mid S)\).
In one or two sentences of words, without formulas: why are the two numbers different?
Are \(S\) and \(R\) independent? One word, then the number that shows it.







NoteSolution




Every employee is equally likely, so Definition 2.1 becomes a ratio of counts: \[
\Prob(S\mid R)=\frac{168}{210}=0.80,\qquad \Prob(R\mid S)=\frac{168}{342}\approx 0.491 .
\]
The numerator is the same, 168 people, but the group we look inside is not. The first number asks what share of remote workers are satisfied. The second asks what share of satisfied people work remotely, and since most of the firm sits in the office, the satisfied group is split almost half and half even though remote workers are happier. It is the swap from Example 2.1.
No. \(\Prob(S)=342/500=0.684\), while \(\Prob(S\mid R)=0.80\). For independent events these two would be equal (Definition 2.2). In the office the share is \(174/290=0.60\).

Two warnings. The table does not say that working from home makes people happier. It could go the other way: managers may let their most satisfied people go remote. And whether a gap like 0.80 against 0.60 in one survey could be chance is a question for a test we meet in module 3.

import pandas as pd

survey = pd.DataFrame({"satisfied": [168, 174], "not satisfied": [42, 116]},
                      index=["remote", "office"])
n_total = survey.values.sum()
both = survey.loc["remote", "satisfied"]
print(f"P(S | R) = {both / survey.loc['remote'].sum():.3f}")
print(f"P(R | S) = {both / survey['satisfied'].sum():.3f}")
print(f"P(S)     = {survey['satisfied'].sum() / n_total:.3f}")

P(S | R) = 0.800
P(R | S) = 0.491
P(S)     = 0.684

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 2
Zarina is at the New Year party of a logistics company in Tyumen. The raffle box holds 40 tickets. Four of them win something: a weekend in Sochi, two pairs of headphones and a cake. She draws 3 tickets, one after another, and does not put any back.

What is the probability that she wins nothing?
What is the probability that she wins exactly one prize?

Solve both with a probability tree (you only need to draw the branches you use). Then check both answers by counting, as in Lecture 1.






NoteSolution



Let \(W_i\) be “ticket \(i\) wins” and \(N_i\) “ticket \(i\) does not win”.

The path \(N_1N_2N_3\). After each losing ticket there is one ticket fewer in the box and one losing ticket fewer. By Equation 2.1, \[
\Prob(N_1\cap N_2\cap N_3)=\frac{36}{40}\cdot\frac{35}{39}\cdot\frac{34}{38}=\frac{42\,840}{59\,280}=\frac{357}{494}\approx 0.723 .
\]
Three paths end with exactly one prize: \(W_1N_2N_3\), \(N_1W_2N_3\) and \(N_1N_2W_3\). For example, \[
\Prob(N_1\cap W_2\cap N_3)=\frac{36}{40}\cdot\frac{4}{39}\cdot\frac{35}{38}=\frac{5040}{59\,280}.
\] The other two paths have the same numbers in a different order, so the same product. The paths are mutually exclusive, and \[
\Prob(\text{exactly one})=3\cdot\frac{5040}{59\,280}=\frac{15\,120}{59\,280}=\frac{63}{247}\approx 0.255 .
\]

Check by counting, exactly as in Example 2.3. Order does not matter, so the outcomes are the \(\binom{40}{3}=9880\) sets of three tickets (Definition 1.8). No prize: \(\binom{36}{3}=7140\) sets, and \(7140/9880=357/494\). Exactly one prize: \(\binom41\binom{36}{2}=4\cdot630=2520\) sets, and \(2520/9880=63/247\). Same answers.
The usual mistake is to use \(4/40\) at every step, as if tickets went back into the box. That gives \(3\cdot0.1\cdot0.9^2=0.243\) for (b), close but wrong.

from math import comb

p_none = (36 / 40) * (35 / 39) * (34 / 38)            # chain rule
p_one = 3 * (36 / 40) * (4 / 39) * (35 / 38)          # three paths
count_none = comb(36, 3) / comb(40, 3)
count_one = comb(4, 1) * comb(36, 2) / comb(40, 3)
print(f"P(no prize)          = {p_none:.3f}, by counting {count_none:.3f}")
print(f"P(exactly one prize) = {p_one:.3f}, by counting {count_one:.3f}")

P(no prize)          = 0.723, by counting 0.723
P(exactly one prize) = 0.255, by counting 0.255

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 3
Short drill, if time allows.
A furniture delivery firm in Samara keeps a record of two kinds of trouble with an order: the sofa or wardrobe arrives damaged, or it arrives late. Let \(D\) be “the item arrives damaged”, usually a scratch picked up while loading the van, and \(L\) “the delivery is late”. Last month’s records give \[
\Prob(D)=0.10,\qquad \Prob(L)=0.20,\qquad \Prob(D\cap L)=0.02 .
\]

Are \(D\) and \(L\) independent? Find \(\Prob(L\mid D)\) as well.
Find the probability that an order had at least one of the two problems, and the probability that it had neither.
Optional, if time allows. At a second firm, the driver checks every item at the customer’s door. A damaged item is not handed over: the delivery is cancelled and a new item is sent later as a new order, so a delivery with a damaged item is never recorded as late. Again \(\Prob(D)=0.10\) and \(\Prob(L)=0.20\). Answer (a) and (b) for this firm and say what has changed.







NoteSolution




\(\Prob(D)\Prob(L)=0.10\cdot0.20=0.02=\Prob(D\cap L)\), so \(D\) and \(L\) are independent by Definition 2.2. In conditional form, \(\Prob(L\mid D)=0.02/0.10=0.20=\Prob(L)\): learning that the item was damaged does not change the chance that the delivery was late. That fits the story, because scratches come from loading in the warehouse and delays come from traffic.
At least one: \(\Prob(D\cup L)=0.10+0.20-0.02=0.28\) (Theorem 1.2). Neither: by Theorem 2.3, \(D^c\) and \(L^c\) are independent too, so \(\Prob(D^c\cap L^c)=0.90\cdot0.80=0.72\), which is \(1-0.28\) as it should be.
Now \(D\) and \(L\) are mutually exclusive, \(\Prob(D\cap L)=0\). That is not \(0.02\), so they are not independent. \(\Prob(L\mid D)=0\): once you know the item was damaged, you know the delivery was not recorded as late. At least one: \(0.10+0.20=0.30\). Neither: \(1-0.30=0.70\). The product \(0.90\cdot0.80=0.72\) is wrong here, because Theorem 2.3 needs independence.


p_damaged, p_late = 0.10, 0.20
for firm, p_both in [("firm 1", 0.02), ("firm 2", 0.00)]:
    p_either = p_damaged + p_late - p_both
    print(f"{firm}: P(L | D) = {p_both / p_damaged:.2f}, "
          f"P(at least one) = {p_either:.2f}, P(neither) = {1 - p_either:.2f}")

firm 1: P(L | D) = 0.20, P(at least one) = 0.28, P(neither) = 0.72
firm 2: P(L | D) = 0.00, P(at least one) = 0.30, P(neither) = 0.70

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 4
Short drill, if time allows.
Find the mistakes. The problem was:

A cinema chain in Tver sells its tickets through a website that runs on two servers in two different data centres. On a given day each server fails with probability 0.05. The site goes down only if both servers fail. What is the probability that the site goes down on a given day?

Gleb from the IT department wrote this solution.

Let \(A\) be “server 1 fails” and \(B\) “server 2 fails”. The site goes down when \(A\cap B\) happens. By the definition of conditional probability, \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A\mid B)/\Prob(B)\). Server 1 fails with probability 0.05 whatever server 2 does, so \(\Prob(A\mid B)=0.05\). Then \(\Prob(A\cap B)=0.05/0.05=1\). The site goes down every day, and the second server does not help at all.


There are two mistakes, one in a formula and one in what Gleb does not say. Find both and give the correct answer.
To save money, the chain moves both servers into one data centre with a single power supply. Does the probability that the site goes down go up, go down or stay the same? No number needed.







NoteSolution




The formula. Definition 2.1 says \(\Prob(A\mid B)=\Prob(A\cap B)/\Prob(B)\). Multiplying both sides by \(\Prob(B)\) gives \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A\mid B)\,\Prob(B)\), which is Theorem 2.2. Gleb divided by \(\Prob(B)\) where he should have multiplied by it. A quick check shows that something is wrong: \(A\cap B\) is inside \(A\), so \(\Prob(A\cap B)\le\Prob(A)=0.05\) by Theorem 1.2. An answer of 1 cannot be right.

What is not said. “Server 1 fails with probability 0.05 whatever server 2 does” means \(\Prob(A\mid B)=\Prob(A)\), which is the assumption that \(A\) and \(B\) are independent (Definition 2.2). The assumption is reasonable here, since the servers sit in different data centres, but it is an assumption. A solution has to say it, and say why it is believable.
Correct answer, assuming independence: \[
\Prob(A\cap B)=0.05\cdot0.05=0.0025,
\] about one day in 400. The simulation below gives the same number, up to random variation.

It goes up. With one power supply, a power cut takes down both servers at once. Then learning that server 2 failed makes it more likely that server 1 failed too, so \(\Prob(A\mid B)>0.05\) and \(\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A\mid B)\Prob(B)>0.0025\). If, say, half of server 2’s failures were power cuts, \(\Prob(A\mid B)\) would be at least 0.5 and the site would go down at least ten times as often.


import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_days, p_fail = 1_000_000, 0.05
server1_down = rng.random(n_days) < p_fail
server2_down = rng.random(n_days) < p_fail  # drawn separately: independent
p_site_down = np.mean(server1_down & server2_down)
print(f"simulated P(site down) = {p_site_down:.4f}, formula = {p_fail * p_fail:.4f}")

simulated P(site down) = 0.0024, formula = 0.0025

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 5
Timur buys online ads for a flower delivery service in Moscow. From a year of data he knows that 30% of the clicks from one ad channel turn into an order. Treat clicks from different people as mutually independent. On the Monday before 8 March, the first six clicks of the day all turn into orders.

Is the seventh click more likely than 30% to turn into an order? One word, then one line.
On Sunday evening, what was the probability that the first six clicks on Monday would all convert?
What was the probability that at least one of the first six would not convert?
Optional, if time allows. Timur’s manager says: “Six orders in a row! This channel suddenly sells much better, double the budget!” What would you look at before you agree or disagree?







NoteSolution




No. Under the model the clicks are mutually independent, so by Definition 2.3 the conditional probability that click 7 converts, given that clicks 1 to 6 did, is still \(0.30\). It is Example 2.4(c) again, with clicks in place of coin tosses.
By Definition 2.3, \(0.3^6=0.000729\), about 7 in 10,000.
The complement of (b): \(1-0.000729=0.999271\). Read the question carefully: “at least one does not convert” is not “none converts”. The second would be \(0.7^6\approx0.118\).
Part (b) is the interesting number. Six conversions in a row has probability about 0.0007 if the model is right, which is rare enough to make you doubt the model. Something may have changed. The days before 8 March are the busiest week of the year for flowers, so people who click on a flower ad that week probably buy much more often than 30%. A tracking bug that counts one order six times is another candidate. If the rate itself has gone up, the manager may be right, though the reason is the season and not the streak: the 30% from ordinary months does not apply this week. Problem 9*(d) shows how Bayes’ theorem updates a belief like this, one observation at a time.

The simulation below agrees with (a) and (b), up to random variation. Only about 1,500 of the two million simulated Mondays have a streak, so the last line rests on far fewer cases than the first and is the least precise.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
p_convert, n_mondays = 0.30, 2_000_000
clicks = rng.random((n_mondays, 7)) < p_convert   # True = order
streak = clicks[:, :6].all(axis=1)                # first six all converted
print(f"P(first six convert) = {streak.mean():.5f}, formula = {p_convert**6:.5f}")
print(f"Mondays with a streak: {streak.sum()}")
print(f"P(7th converts | streak) = {clicks[streak, 6].mean():.3f}")

P(first six convert) = 0.00075, formula = 0.00073
Mondays with a streak: 1490
P(7th converts | streak) = 0.299

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 6
Calls to the support line of an online electronics shop go to three call centres: 50% to Kazan, 30% to Ufa and 20% to Izhevsk. The Izhevsk centre opened in the spring, and most of its staff are still on probation, the trial months of a new job. A call ends with a written complaint in 1% of cases in Kazan, 2% in Ufa and 4% in Izhevsk.
What share of all calls ends with a complaint?






NoteSolution



Let \(H_1\), \(H_2\), \(H_3\) be “the call went to Kazan”, “to Ufa”, “to Izhevsk”. Every call goes to exactly one centre, so these three events form a partition. Let \(K\) be “the call ends with a complaint”. By Equation 2.2, \[
\Prob(K)=0.01\cdot0.50+0.02\cdot0.30+0.04\cdot0.20=0.005+0.006+0.008=0.019 ,
\] so 1.9% of calls. In counts: of 10,000 calls, 5000 go to Kazan and 50 of them end with a complaint, 3000 go to Ufa with 60 complaints, and 2000 go to Izhevsk with 80. That is 190 complaints in 10,000 calls.
A quick check: by Theorem 2.4 the answer is a weighted average of 1%, 2% and 4%, an average in which each rate counts as much as its centre’s share of calls. So anything outside the range from 1% to 4% would be wrong.

import numpy as np

share = np.array([0.50, 0.30, 0.20])              # Kazan, Ufa, Izhevsk
p_complaint_given = np.array([0.01, 0.02, 0.04])
p_complaint = np.sum(share * p_complaint_given)
print(f"P(complaint) = {p_complaint:.3f}")
kazan, ufa, izhevsk = np.round(10_000 * share * p_complaint_given).astype(int)
print(f"Complaints per 10,000 calls: Kazan {kazan}, Ufa {ufa}, Izhevsk {izhevsk}")

P(complaint) = 0.019
Complaints per 10,000 calls: Kazan 50, Ufa 60, Izhevsk 80
crumbs: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 7
Continue Problem 6. A written complaint reaches head office, and it does not say which centre took the call. Aigerim, the quality manager, will listen to the recordings of one centre first.

Find the probability that the call went to each of the three centres. Which centre should Aigerim start with?
In (a), Izhevsk takes only 20% of the calls, yet it is the most likely source. Explain why in one sentence.
Next year the shop sends 70% of the calls to Kazan, 20% to Ufa and 10% to Izhevsk. The complaint rates stay the same. Answer (a) again.







NoteSolution




By Equation 2.3, with the denominator \(\Prob(K)=0.019\) from Problem 6, \[
\Prob(H_1\mid K)=\frac{0.005}{0.019}=\frac{5}{19}\approx0.263,\quad
\Prob(H_2\mid K)=\frac{0.006}{0.019}=\frac{6}{19}\approx0.316,\quad
\Prob(H_3\mid K)=\frac{0.008}{0.019}=\frac{8}{19}\approx0.421 .
\] The counts from Problem 6 say the same: of 190 complaints, 50, 60 and 80 came from the three centres. The three answers add up to 1, which is a free check. Aigerim should start with Izhevsk.
Its complaint rate is four times that of Kazan, and that beats its share of calls being 2.5 times smaller: \(0.20\cdot0.04=0.008\) against \(0.50\cdot0.01=0.005\).
New denominator: \(\Prob(K)=0.01\cdot0.70+0.02\cdot0.20+0.04\cdot0.10=0.007+0.004+0.004=0.015\). Then \[
\Prob(H_1\mid K)=\frac{0.007}{0.015}\approx0.467,\qquad
\Prob(H_2\mid K)=\Prob(H_3\mid K)=\frac{0.004}{0.015}\approx0.267 .
\] Now Kazan is the most likely source, and Aigerim should start there. The complaint rates are the same as before; only the priors moved.


import numpy as np

centres = ["Kazan", "Ufa", "Izhevsk"]
p_complaint_given = np.array([0.01, 0.02, 0.04])
for share in ([0.50, 0.30, 0.20], [0.70, 0.20, 0.10]):
    joint = np.array(share) * p_complaint_given     # P(K and H_i)
    posterior = joint / joint.sum()                 # Bayes: divide by P(K)
    print(f"Shares of calls {share}, P(complaint) = {joint.sum():.3f}:")
    for centre, p in zip(centres, posterior):
        print(f"  P(call went to {centre} | complaint) = {p:.3f}")

Shares of calls [0.5, 0.3, 0.2], P(complaint) = 0.019:
  P(call went to Kazan | complaint) = 0.263
  P(call went to Ufa | complaint) = 0.316
  P(call went to Izhevsk | complaint) = 0.421
Shares of calls [0.7, 0.2, 0.1], P(complaint) = 0.015:
  P(call went to Kazan | complaint) = 0.467
  P(call went to Ufa | complaint) = 0.267
  P(call went to Izhevsk | complaint) = 0.267

text:
Problem 8
At a consumer-loan bank in Krasnoyarsk, 5% of clients default, that is, do not repay. Diego from the credit-risk team is testing a scoring model. On old clients, the model flagged 80% of those who later defaulted and 10% of those who repaid.

Imagine 10,000 applicants. Fill in a table with rows “default” and “repay”, columns “flagged” and “not flagged”, and totals.
A sales manager reads the test report and says: “The model catches 80% of defaulters, so a flagged client defaults with probability 0.8.” Find the correct probability with Bayes’ theorem and check it in your table.
What share of the clients who are not flagged default?

title: Seminar 2: conditional probability, independence and Bayes
text:
Problem 9*
This problem goes beyond Lecture 2 and is not examinable. It uses Bayes’ theorem several times in a row, and the new idea is simple: after each piece of evidence, the posterior becomes the prior for the next one.

Diego’s bank from Problem 8 (default rate 5%) adds a second check, a report from a credit bureau. The report comes out “bad” for 70% of the clients who will default and for 20% of the clients who will repay. Assume that the model and the bureau report are conditionally independent given the type of client. In plain words: among defaulters, a bad report is no more and no less likely for flagged clients than for unflagged ones, and the same holds among clients who repay. The model looks at the application form and the bureau at old loans, so once you know what kind of client it is, one check tells you nothing new about the other.

An applicant is flagged by the model. Take the answer of Problem 8(b) as the new prior. What is the probability of default if the bureau report is bad? If it is clean?

Check the “bad report” answer in one step. Find the probability that a defaulter is both flagged and has a bad report, the same for a client who repays, and apply Bayes’ theorem once with the prior 0.05.
Now the money. Every client borrows 300,000 rubles. A default costs the bank 200,000 rubles (it gets part of the money back), and a repaid loan earns 30,000 rubles of interest. The bank compares two rules with lending to everyone:


Rule 1: reject every applicant the model flags.
Rule 2: for a flagged applicant, also get the bureau report, and reject only if it is bad.

For 10,000 applicants, how much loss does each rule avoid, how much interest does it give up, and what is the difference? Which rule is better? Ignore the price of the bureau reports.

Lecture 2 left one case open: a firm rejected by five banks in a row (Independence). Suppose that 20% of the small firms that apply for loans are poor payers and 80% are ordinary. A bank rejects a poor payer with probability 0.90 and an ordinary firm with probability 0.65, so overall it rejects \(0.2\cdot0.90+0.8\cdot0.65=0.70\) of applications, like the loan officer in the lecture. Given the type of firm, different banks decide conditionally independently. One firm is rejected by bank after bank. Find the probability that it is a poor payer after each of the first five rejections. Then find the probability that a sixth bank also rejects it.
Is the conditional independence in (d) believable? One or two sentences.







NoteSolution




The prior is now \(\Prob(D\mid F)=0.04/0.135=8/27\approx0.296\), and \(\Prob(D^c\mid F)=19/27\). Let \(R\) be “the report is bad”. Conditional independence says that \(\Prob(R\mid D\cap F)=\Prob(R\mid D)=0.70\) and \(\Prob(R\mid D^c\cap F)=\Prob(R\mid D^c)=0.20\), so Equation 2.3 is used exactly as before, only with the new prior: \[
\Prob(D\mid F\cap R)=\frac{0.70\cdot\frac{8}{27}}{0.70\cdot\frac{8}{27}+0.20\cdot\frac{19}{27}}=\frac{5.6}{5.6+3.8}=\frac{28}{47}\approx0.596 .
\] A clean report has probability 0.30 for defaulters and 0.80 for good clients: \[
\Prob(D\mid F\cap R^c)=\frac{0.30\cdot\frac{8}{27}}{0.30\cdot\frac{8}{27}+0.80\cdot\frac{19}{27}}=\frac{2.4}{2.4+15.2}=\frac{3}{22}\approx0.136 .
\] Both signals together take the applicant from 5% to about 60%. A flag with a clean report leaves about 14%, still well above the 5% we started from.
By conditional independence, \(\Prob(F\cap R\mid D)=0.80\cdot0.70=0.56\) and \(\Prob(F\cap R\mid D^c)=0.10\cdot0.20=0.02\). Then \[
\Prob(D\mid F\cap R)=\frac{0.56\cdot0.05}{0.56\cdot0.05+0.02\cdot0.95}=\frac{0.028}{0.028+0.019}=\frac{28}{47},
\] the same as updating twice. The order of the two checks does not matter either.

The flag and the bad report are not independent events. \(\Prob(F)=0.135\) and \(\Prob(R)=0.70\cdot0.05+0.20\cdot0.95=0.225\), whose product is about 0.030, while \(\Prob(F\cap R)=0.028+0.019=0.047\). Both checks react to the same hidden thing, the type of client. Independence given the type and independence are different statements.

Start from the table of Problem 8(a): 400 of the 500 defaulters and 950 of the 9,500 good clients are flagged.

Rule 1 avoids 400 defaults, \(400\cdot200{,}000=80{,}000{,}000\) rubles, and rejects 950 good clients, who would have paid \(950\cdot30{,}000=28{,}500{,}000\) rubles of interest. The net gain for the bank is \(51{,}500{,}000\) rubles.
Rule 2. By conditional independence, the report is bad for 70% of the 400 flagged defaulters, which is 280, and for 20% of the 950 flagged good clients, which is 190. The rule avoids \(280\cdot200{,}000=56{,}000{,}000\) rubles and gives up \(190\cdot30{,}000=5{,}700{,}000\). The net gain is \(50{,}300{,}000\) rubles.
Rule 1 wins, by 1.2 million rubles. The two rules differ only on the 880 flagged applicants with a clean report, 120 defaulters and 760 good clients. Rule 2 lends to them: it earns \(760\cdot30{,}000=22{,}800{,}000\) rubles and loses \(120\cdot200{,}000=24{,}000{,}000\). In probabilities, their default rate is \(3/22\approx0.136\) from (a), and lending to a group pays only if its default rate is below \(30{,}000/230{,}000\approx0.130\). So with these prices the bank should reject a flagged applicant even when the report is clean, and the bureau report is not worth buying for this decision. With 32,000 rubles of interest per loan instead of 30,000, the break-even rate would be \(32{,}000/232{,}000\approx0.138\), and Rule 2 would win.

Let \(P\) be “poor payer”, with prior \(\Prob(P)=0.20\). After the first rejection, by Equation 2.3, \[
\Prob(P\mid\text{1 rejection})=\frac{0.90\cdot0.20}{0.90\cdot0.20+0.65\cdot0.80}=\frac{0.18}{0.70}\approx0.257 .
\] This becomes the prior for the second rejection, and so on. Each step takes the current \(p\) to \(0.90p/\big(0.90p+0.65(1-p)\big)\):

For the sixth bank, use Equation 2.2 with the current beliefs as weights: \[
\Prob(\text{6th rejects}\mid\text{5 rejections})=0.90\cdot0.560+0.65\cdot0.440\approx0.790,
\] against 0.70 for a firm we know nothing about. So the lecture was right that the sixth bank is not a new toss of a coin. Still, each rejection is weak evidence, since poor payers are rejected only \(0.90/0.65\approx1.4\) times as often as ordinary firms, and even after five rejections the firm is a poor payer with probability only 0.56.

Not fully. Banks buy reports from the same credit bureaux and use similar rules, so even for an ordinary firm one rejection makes the next more likely. Then the five rejections partly repeat one piece of evidence, and 0.56 is too high. If all banks decided exactly alike, five rejections would carry no more information than one, and the answer would be 0.257. The real answer lies between 0.257 and 0.56.

A simulation of one million applicants for (a) and (b). The bureau report is drawn separately from the flag, given the client’s type, which is exactly conditional independence.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_clients = 1_000_000
default = rng.random(n_clients) < 0.05
flagged = rng.random(n_clients) < np.where(default, 0.80, 0.10)
bad_report = rng.random(n_clients) < np.where(default, 0.70, 0.20)
print(f"P(D | flagged, bad report)   = {default[flagged & bad_report].mean():.3f}")
print(f"P(D | flagged, clean report) = {default[flagged & ~bad_report].mean():.3f}")

# share of defaulters and of good clients that each rule rejects

for rule, (reject_default, reject_repay) in rules.items():
    avoided = round(reject_default * n_default) * cost_default
    given_up = round(reject_repay * n_repay) * interest

          f"net gain {avoided - given_up:,} rubles")
